articles.title: Beyond Plantation Capitalism
articles.author: Dick Price, Sharon Kyle, Peter Laarman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. An interview with Rev. Peter Laarman by Dick Price and Sharon Kyle What will it take to dismantle an economic system that concentrates extraordinary wealth in the hands of a tiny elite while millions of working people struggle to survive? And how do we build a movement capable of changing not only the policies that sustain inequality but also the values that make such inequality seem acceptable? These questions were at the center of a recent LA Progressive conversation with Rev. Peter Laarman, a retired minister who formerly led Progressive Christians Uniting in Los Angeles. A member of the National Council of Elders, Laarman also serves on its King and Breaking Silence team. Speaking with LA Progressive co-founders Dick Price and Sharon Kyle about his article, Curbing Cancerous Capitalism: An Organizing Challenge for the Ages , Laarman explored the enduring influence of racial hierarchy, the economic legacy of slavery, and the challenge of building a movement that confronts both. Plantation Capitalism (27:12) The Legacy of Plantation Capitalism Central to Laarman's argument is a phrase frequently invoked by the late Rev. James Lawson Jr., the legendary civil rights strategist and advocate of radical nonviolence: "plantation capitalism." Laarman knew Lawson through their overlapping work in Los Angeles, including labor organizing and economic justice initiatives. Lawson had been instrumental in the Justice for Janitors campaign and Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice, helping connect struggles for workers' rights with a broader movement for social transformation. For Lawson, plantation capitalism was not simply a reference to the historical plantation economy. It described an enduring relationship between concentrated economic power and the people whose labor generates wealth. "The real point," Laarman explained, "is the default wage for most of the history of people on this continent was zero," referring to the uncompensated labor imposed through chattel slavery. He argued that the assumption among powerful interests that labor should cost as little as possible never disappeared with emancipation. Kyle connected that observation to contemporary wage labor, noting that although chattel slavery and wage employment are fundamentally different legal arrangements, both raise questions about who controls the wealth produced by workers. Laarman agreed that wage labor is inherently extractive under capitalism, pointing to the growing concentration of economic power. The conversation turned to the industrial transformation that accompanied the Civil War era. Laarman described how skilled workers in the 1840s and 1850s valued their independence and feared that emerging factory systems would strip them of economic autonomy. He also emphasized that opposition to slavery's expansion did not necessarily translate into support for Black equality. Related: Marlon James Uncovers Depths of Depravity in Evangelical Christianity The Two Walls That Defeated Reconstruction Laarman identified two major forces that undermined the promise of Reconstruction. The first was white racial resentment, particularly resistance to repairing the enormous harm inflicted through slavery. The second was Wall Street's determination to industrialize the nation and exploit its resources following the Civil War. Many northern industrialists who had supported abolition were nevertheless unwilling to support meaningful economic restitution for formerly enslaved people. Instead, Laarman argued, they accepted the continuing racial caste system because it served the interests of industrial capitalism. That history reveals a distinction too often obscured in American accounts of emancipation: ending the legal ownership of human beings did not end the struggle over who controlled labor, property, and the wealth labor produced. Kyle drew a connection between that history and today's extraordinary concentrations of private wealth, questioning why the economic contributions of millions of workers are so routinely attributed to a handful of billionaires. Electoral Victories Are Not Enough The discussion then moved from history to the political challenges confronting the United States today. Laarman warned against assuming that Democratic electoral victories, however welcome, would produce the fundamental changes required to confront inequality and racial domination. Even a sweeping Democratic victory, he suggested, could encourage complacency among comfortable constituencies. He worried that political leaders might leave intact extraordinary executive powers, expansive immigration enforcement structures, and the economic arrangements that direct wealth upward. The danger, he argued, is that temporary political relief could substitute for lasting structural change. "I firmly believe that a transformed politics has to follow a transformed culture," Laarman said, describing the work ahead as both a spiritual and psychological challenge. But he rejected the notion that people should wait for some sweeping moral awakening before acting. Immediate resistance remains essential, particularly in defending vulnerable communities, building mutual aid networks, and exposing the influence of wealthy political donors. Related: Chattel Slavery vs. Wage Labor: Who Is Really Free? The Search for a Different Kind of Movement Kyle pressed Laarman on a question that has become increasingly urgent for those who recognize the depth of America's problems: Where are the organizations that understand the structural nature of economic and racial domination and are actually developing ways to overcome it? Laarman acknowledged that the answer remains incomplete. He described emerging initiatives seeking to connect organizers, abolitionist movements, and communities committed to social transformation. Within the National Council of Elders, he said, discussions are underway about developing local "begin-again circles." These gatherings would offer activists something different from another meeting, campaign, or organizational obligation. They would provide spaces for reflection, renewal, trust, and meaningful connection. Laarman envisioned places where participants could be vulnerable, where everyone would be heard, and where spiritual nourishment would not depend on religious affiliation. Such spaces, he suggested, could help sustain people engaged in exhausting struggles against entrenched power. He also pointed to historical moments when profound cultural changes accompanied political transformation, including the struggles in Poland, Czechoslovakia, and South Africa. Although no example guarantees a lasting transformation, these experiences demonstrate that deeply established systems of domination are not necessarily permanent. Challenging the Wealthy to See Their Common Interests Price raised another formidable obstacle: America's affluent professional and business classes, many of whom benefit substantially from the existing system. Laarman acknowledged that this group represents an important political constituency whose members frequently identify with billionaires rather than working people. Yet he argued that smaller business owners and millionaires are increasingly vulnerable to the same concentrations of economic power, particularly through private equity and emerging technologies. The organizing challenge is to persuade them that their interests are not necessarily aligned with those of the ultrawealthy. That may prove difficult in a culture that encourages people to imagine themselves as future billionaires, even when the economic system makes such outcomes extraordinarily unlikely. Related: Recalling the Torments of a Radical Truthteller Reaching for a Higher Plane Throughout the conversation, Laarman returned to Lawson's conviction that economic justice cannot be separated from the moral and spiritual condition of society. His argument was not that political organizing should give way to religious reflection. Rather, the two must reinforce each other. Movements need practical strategies, durable institutions, and the power to resist exploitation. But they also need a shared understanding of human dignity strong enough to challenge a culture that treats unlimited accumulation as an unquestioned virtue. For Laarman, the task is neither to dismiss existing movements nor to wait for a perfect new organization to appear. It is to connect struggles already underway while inviting participants to imagine a more profound transformation. "We're gonna reach higher," he said. "We're not gonna piss on other people's efforts, but we're going to invite people to step up to a higher plane." The challenge raised by Lawson's concept of plantation capitalism remains: Can Americans build an economy in which the people who create society's wealth also share meaningfully in its benefits and exercise power over the conditions of their lives? Laarman does not pretend to have a complete blueprint. But his insistence that structural change must be accompanied by cultural transformation offers a direction for those determined to move beyond simply managing an unjust system. The task is not merely to curb capitalism's most destructive excesses. It is to organize a society in which human dignity matters more than the unchecked accumulation of wealth.

articles.title: OPINION: No on Q3 – Jungle Primaries are Bad for Working People’s Interests
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: Boston during a nor’easter approaching Election Day (Working Mass) By: Jonathan Cohn The most dangerous words in the English language are: “we’re from private equity, and we’re here to help.” When private equity swoops in to “help” a struggling business, that typically means worsening labor conditions and worsening product quality—but increasing the money of those private equity executives. That’s exactly what private equity executives are trying to do with democracy in Massachusetts with this year’s Question 3, making it a place where they can more easily buy candidates and forestall progressive victories at the state and federal level. These donors are seeking to curb the rise of more populist messaging and policy that centers working people rather than the rich and large corporations. The fact that jungle primaries are detrimental to workers’ interests is why labor unions and progressive groups across Massachusetts are united in urging you to vote NO on Question 3. Question 3 would change MA’s electoral system to a jungle primary system like California and Washington. Proponents have been saying that this is about democracy, accountability, choice, competition, but a quick look at where the money comes from says otherwise. According to campaign finance disclosures, 70% of the money raised for Question 3 comes from private equity, with most of that from Bain Capital or Berkshire Partners. Indeed, just six private equity executives account for half of all the money raised by the campaign. These are overwhelmingly donors to conservative Democrats (like MA’s Jake Auchincloss and Seth Moulton) and Republicans (like Susan Collins and Bill Cassidy) who are friendly to the corporate centrism that the financial industry loves. These donors have a long history of funding education privatization ballot questions, and not a lot of history caring about democracy. What is Q3? Question 3 makes several noteworthy changes to Massachusetts elections. It’s important to understand the risks of all of them. The marquis part of Question 3 is the all-party primary system, often called a jungle primary, in which all candidates run on the same ballot and the top two candidates of any party advance to the general election. More on that in a moment. Question 3 also changes how MA elects Lieutenant Governors. Currently, MA has a system with the perhaps inartful moniker of “shotgun marriage”: Governor and Lt. Governor candidates run separately in the primary, and then are paired together in the general election. Under Question 3, gubernatorial candidates would pick their running mates upon formally filing as a candidate with the Secretary of State. Vetting possible running mates is a major hurdle for grassroots and less institutionally connected candidates, and if people don’t think you can win (grassroots candidates often peak late), why would anyone want to bet a year of their time on your campaign? It’s a very clear way to limit the possibility of who can consider running. Question 3 also changes ballot design in Massachusetts. In a bastardized version of fusion voting, it allows multiple minor parties to endorse the same candidate on the ballot. Fusion voting in states like New York strengthens democracy by enabling voters to choose minor parties’ ballot lines and help them to build a base. They earn that ballot line by having actual voters. By contrast, in Massachusetts, you can get minor party status with only 50 people petitioning the secretary of state. With such a low threshold, any slumlord can create a minor party (say, “Massachusetts Housing for All”), and start endorsing candidates on the ballot with deceptive names. The SuperPACs that flood your mailboxes in election season have to disclose their donors, but imagine if they can just get their endorsements printed directly on your ballot. An empty store (Working Mass) A Warning From California California’s recent gubernatorial primary should be a warning to anyone thinking about voting YES on Question 3 this November. This year, given the diverse Democratic field and narrow Republican field in the gubernatorial race, polling consistently showed that two conservative Republicans would advance to the general election, denying voters real choice. Out of fear of such a lockout, the CA Democratic Party started pressuring candidates to drop out of the race, and the two dominant candidates became a self-funding billionaire and the candidate backed by every corporate PAC in the state. Actual policy debate was sidelined, and party elites and big money donors were empowered. Whenever there is a push for consolidation, those with power, money, and privilege will always claim a right to stay in a race, regardless of whether they have the best ideas (often, they don’t). One of the biggest advocates for California’s jungle primary system has been the California Chamber of Commerce . They have touted its ability to help them get more corporate-aligned Democrats elected on the basis of lots of outside special interest money, conservative crossover votes in Democrat vs. Democrat general elections, and the loss of cues through which people typically understand the differences between candidates. And they are right, with the emergence of a new bloc of corporate-backed Democrats more loyal to Uber, Chevron, Meta, and crypto than to any constituencies or values. That’s not a solution to any problem we have in Massachusetts; it will make the ability to pass policies to help working people even harder. Getting Diverse, Working-Class Candidates to Run I have worked for many years to try to recruit more candidates to run for office and support them when they do. When I talk with prospective candidates, the two biggest barriers for them when considering running for office are time and money. Running for office takes up a lot of time. It might require you to take an extended leave from work, or balance a full-time campaign and a full-time job. It also costs a lot of money to run for office, and most people don’t start out with a readymade list of high-net-worth donor prospects. If we want to see more working people run for office, then we need to find ways to rein in the time and financial burdens of running for office. Question 3 makes both of them worse, increasing both the time and money involved in running for office–benefiting incumbents and wealthy candidates for whom neither poses a true obstacle. Ranked Choice Voting vs. Jungle Primaries Although Massachusetts voters unfortunately rejected Ranked Choice Voting in 2020, there has been a robust and inspiring push on the local level to adopt Ranked Choice Voting on the local level. The push for a top-two primary system takes the wind out of those sails. New York City’s mayoral race last year showed us the wide-ranging benefits of ranked choice voting. Zohran Mamdani’s Democratic primary was due to an amazing field operation and a compelling message, for sure, but NYC’s Ranked Choice Voting system was essential to how the campaign played out. When voters can pick multiple candidates and register their preferences accordingly, progressive candidates aren’t in a fight to the death: they want each other’s voters to also rank them. We saw that dynamic in 2025’s greatest bromance: the cross-endorsement between Zohran Mamdani and former Comptroller and current Congressman-elect Brad Lander and the positivity and goodwill surrounding it. When progressive candidates lift each other up, the ideas and the movement benefit. In a ranked choice system, voters also don’t need to be afraid that voting for their top choice could lead to their least favorite choice getting elected. If you were a voter who did not want to see Andrew Cuomo become governor, you didn’t need to spend hours agonizing about how others might vote: you just vote for multiple progressive candidates and leave Cuomo off your ballot. A jungle primary, by contrast, is what Andrew Cuomo wanted to jerry-rig New York’s election system into. After losing the primary, he insisted on staying in the election, and he wanted to force out other candidates in order to form a cross-party conservative coalition, backed by a lot of money and a lot of racism. Cuomo was able to strong-arm Mayor Eric Adams out of the general election, but failed to convince Republican candidate Curtis Silwa out. Nonetheless, Cuomo still got 73% of Republican voters to vote for him, according to exit polls . With Mamdani pulling 50.78% of the vote in the general election, one can easily see how Cuomo’s theory of the election could have worked if he bullied his way into a two-party race. Democracy and the City of New York would have been worse for it. Just Say No Question 3 is shaping up to be a “Whose side are you on?” question. On the yes side: private equity, venture capitalists, and investment bankers. On the no side: every major labor union and progressive group in the state. The yes side, bankrolled by those who have been fighting for years to make working people’s lives worse, and the no side, backed by those who have been fighting to make working people’s lives better. The choice is clear: NO on Question 3. Jonathan Cohn is a member of Boston DSA and Policy Director for Progressive Massachusetts, a multi-issue grassroots organization that advocates for state level policy. He has been active in campaigns to expand voting rights, strengthen immigrants’ rights, increase education funding, and make a fairer tax code, among many more. He has also been a volunteer, neighborhood team leader, regional coordinator, or campaign manager for various candidate campaigns and ballot initiatives at the city, state, county, and national level. articles.title: The Unhinged Racist Response to France’s School Protests
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content: After protests and riots swept France this weekend following the escalating social movement sparked by high schooler blockades, right-wingers internationally responded with a straightforwardly racist narrative. They’re portraying the protests as the work of Muslim invaders, in a treasonous alliance with astroturfed left-wingers, who are working to torch the country. “France is burning!” Donald Trump reacted . “The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen,” Trump’s vice president, JD Vance, posted in reaction to a video of the bell tower of the Limoges Town Hall falling in flames. “I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn. And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.” The narrative ignores any of the popular demands, including France’s out-of-control cost of living, a degraded school system, and legitimate explosive anger over the murderous violence the police unleashed on high schoolers at the beginning of the month. Since the movement began, replacing such concerns with blind-to-reality, downright racist grievance-mongering has been the official line taken by international reaction. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration,” Trump posted to an official White House government account early this month, as the movement started making global headlines. “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” “Europe opened its borders and failed to confront radical Islamism,” Texas Senator Ted Cruz commented then. “AOC, Mamdani, El-Sayed, and Talarico want to take us in this direction.” “We need to recognize that the pro-Palestinian protests are fundamentally protests against the West, and their ambitions are much greater than eradicating Israel from the river to the sea,” hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman bloviated in response to a chairwoman of a Berlin-based think tank describing a video of protesters chanting “We’re all children of Gaza” as the beginning of an “Islamic Revolution in Europe.” “In Iran, it took roughly two years to go from this stage to complete chaos and the establishment of the Islamic Republic,” that chairwoman, Maral Salmassi, who helms the Zera Institute, wrote . “We saw the same symbolism, the same flags, and heard the exact same slogans. Brace yourselves.” Fox News echoed and boosted the theme early on, publishing an investigation on October 9 attempting to delegitimize the student movement by portraying it as a global conspiracy between communists and Islamists. “A transnational network of 50 groups mobilizes around student protests, only 1/3 are youth groups,” read the breathless subheading of the piece, which claimed to have uncovered a globe-spanning operation of “far-left communist and socialist organizations” who are using the “fiery student protests” to push a “political and ideological agenda.” France’s hysterical racists, boosted by far-right American media organizations devoted to pushing racist propaganda, also weighed in early on. “You have to be blind not to see what’s happening here,” Thaïs d’Escufon, the former spokesperson for the since dissolved French white nationalist group Génération identitaire , told One America News host Chanel Rion, describing the student protests as “ethnic riots.” “They only show footage of the students of the bourgeoisie, of the center of Paris, but actually most of the protests are from cities or areas with a lot of replacement,” d’Escufon explained, using “replaced” to mean areas with a lower percentage of whites. “It’s hard to see this footage. . . . You look at this and it doesn’t look like Paris,” Rion emoted after showing overhead footage of an anonymous crowd of protesters at the Place de la Nation in Paris after a march. “It looks like Mogadishu. . . . And yet you saw the photo that the BBC used. They make it look like it’s just native French students upset by a lack of blackboards.” Fox’s investigation has also endorsed the idea that the media has sanitized the movement by portraying it as “students protesting [against] deteriorating school conditions.” In reality, Fox claimed, the movement “is. . . . part of an extensive infrastructure of unions, communist activists, far-left political parties and international media organizations. . . . [who] are organizing demonstrations, calling strikes, mobilizing supporters and broadcasting the unrest around the world.” Fox’s investigation argues that only fifteen of the fifty organizations involved in the movement are actual student groups, and among those groups are communist youth movements and a Muslim student association. Singling out the communist and Muslim organizations, Fox concludes that there’s a “‘red-green’ alliance of leftists with Muslims.” “The communist Red and the Islamist Greens have nothing in common but a common enemy, the Judeo-Christian, capitalist, free West, led by the U.S.,” Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox. “Their goal is to dismantle us.” British fascist Tommy Robinson has attacked the movement on similar grounds. “The ‘French students’ are destroying Paris again right now,” he joked last week, above a video of French police running past a burning car. This past Wednesday, Robinson attacked Bally Bagayoko, the France Insoumise mayor of Saint-Denis, in a post linking to a video of Bagayoko announcing a restriction on selling alcohol around the city’s train station between 7 pm and 6 am. “Bally Bagayoko made history in March 2026 by becoming the first Black and Muslim mayor mayor of Saint-Denis,” Robinson wrote . “Joined the invader riots last week. Today he announced a ban on alcohol. Wake the fuck up France.” Al-Trojan House The messaging echoes a pernicious narrative in French media that has sought to portray any political organizing by French Muslims as a self-evident Trojan horse for Islamism. “Behind demands about the degraded situation of high schools, the Étudiants musulmans de France (EMF) organization and its allies push their battle against ‘state islamophobia,’” reads a subheading from a story in Le Point claiming that “Islamist networks” are trying to amplify the movement. The article points to a Muslim student organization it claims a government report last year identified as the youth branch of the Muslim Brotherhood. Accusing organizations like EMF of “recuperating” the protests, the article says posts from the organization “speak volumes” about their strategy. One offender from the beginning of the month is a statement in support of the high schoolers’ fight “for a decent and dignified learning environment.” EMF’s statement goes on to oppose government austerity in public services, including universities; a law that raises fees for foreign students; government measures canceling rent subsidies for foreign students; “university partnerships with genocidal and ecocidal businesses”; the selective and “racist” system of university admissions; and government repression of the protests. Le Point also points to AJ+, the Qatari-funded social media wing of Al Jazeera , for their viral social media output highlighting atrocious school conditions and police violence as a vector for spreading this narrative. “Most of them return to the topic of police violence, without a word about the protesters’ [violence], and accuse the ‘mainstream media’ of lying about the ‘violence’ of the marches,” the Le Point article reads. A Liberal Response Massive protests over the weekend of at least a half million people descended into violence, with the police in Paris reportedly losing control of the situation as black bloc militants and vandals took advantage of the chaos to loot some of the city’s toniest quarters. Videos like the clip of the Limoges bell tower falling in flames went viral as examples of destruction being wrought by Third World “barbarians” on Eternal France. “I hope the world is paying attention to the riots in France,” said Tim Kennedy , a celebrity soldier and MMA fighter. “There are no French flags being flown at these protests. This is the consequence of mass immigration.” The idea that there were no French flags being flown at the protests is a flat-out lie. I saw many over multiple days . But the post is representative of the hardening of the narrative laid down earlier in the month. Pro-European liberals also joined in on the hand-wringing and condemnation. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced without making a direct reference to the protests in France. “We are firmly defending the border against illegal migration, we have our own asylum policy (we do not accept applications), we deport those who break Polish law.” “Shocking videos and images are coming out of France,” Hungarian President Péter Magyar posted. “In the face of this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration, and why we will not weaken our border protection or immigration policy under any pressure.” Feckless American liberals, while condemning the straightforwardly racist framing and acknowledging that the student protesters are “an extremely diverse coalition,” have flirted with the narrative. Thomas Chatterton Williams, in a piece in The Atlantic titled “The Violence Sweeping France Was Never Really About Schools,” dismisses any real content in the protests after a review of five viral social media clips. “Much of the protesting by students has become an exercise in nihilistic resentment. . . . beneath the pretext of school reform,” Williams writes, pointing to clips showing acts of violence, property damage, or students rallying and shouting, often from social media aggregator accounts that push an anti-immigrant narrative, frequently portraying Arab and African immigration in Europe as a Trojan horse for Islamism. “The violence hasn’t been limited to one side,” Williams admits charitably, drawing parallels between students making anti-police declarations in crowds or singing along to rap songs with distasteful references to terrorism and life-changing, disfiguring injuries inflicted on students by the police. “A police officer fired a tear gas grenade at a teenager’s head, knocking out most of his teeth. More recently, a 15-year-old lost his hand after an officer fired a stun grenade.” At the end of the day France is “at the mercy of protesters,” Williams argues. “The French protest too much,” and “in recent years, France’s protest culture has been indulged and glorified to the point of insanity.” “Some of these demands may be valid,” Williams allows, “but the violence fanning out across France has little to do with pedagogical concerns.” Protesting Right French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu made a similar argument on Thursday when he claimed that the social movement was “no longer a high schoolers’ movement” but a “movement of urban violence, the intensity of which has increased further in recent days.” In a speech on Sunday evening, President Emmanuel Macron blamed the violence from the night before on “troublemakers from far-left splinter groups, joined by numerous delinquents,” while Lecornu denounced the supposedly “important role” of France Insoumise presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his party in fomenting it. While the French government hasn’t engaged in the same grotesquely racist theories of the American, British, and French far right, they are united with them in their narrative that this social movement is the product of outside, illegitimate forces that are trying to instrumentalize the demands of the high schoolers. That point was driven home particularly forcefully in a report from the Le Canard enchaîné on Wednesday, which revealed that Lecornu had personally directed the interior minister to explore the idea of prosecuting Mélenchon for “inciting rebellion.” Lecornu only backed off after getting cold feet about what type of effect jailing Mélenchon might have on the movement. The paper reported nearly seven thousand arrestees over the past three weeks, 86 percent of whom were between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. Authorities made around two thousand additional arrests over the weekend. “The goal of the tactic is to frighten the students and their parents into stopping the uprising as quickly as possible,” one chief of police told Le Canard . The government remains scared of this social movement because of the fact that it isn’t a foreign plot, the work of immigrant invaders, or an ” Islamo-leftist ” conspiracy. Powerful racists will continue to push the idea that it is because it’s a convenient way to wipe away the demands of the masses, but it won’t change the reality on the ground. Macron’s government has brought violence to France’s streets. A report on Monday morning that Macron rejected the Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign sends a clear message that he supports what the police are doing despite last night’s pro forma calls for dialogue and rote condemnation of violence. French students have legitimate demands, and many of them are determined to continue protesting until the government answers them. articles.title: Joint labor/socialist effort made Tax the Rich Day on October 10 a statewide success
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: California is the fourth largest economy in the world, with a growing number of billionaires, and an expanding crisis of poverty due to concentration of wealth and divestment from public goods like education and healthcare. This has been exacerbated by the Trump administration’s HR1 (“the big beautiful bill”), which cut $1 trillion from Medicaid nationally, resulting in a $100 billion cut to Medi-Cal, and a $20 billion cut to Calfresh, public programs that support our most vulnerable neighbors. After the California Federation of Labor Unions, led by Lorena Gonzalez, voted at its August 4 convention to endorse two ballot measures to tax the rich – Propositions 3 and 40 – California DSA took the opportunity to reach out with a proposal: a California “Tax the Rich Day” on October 10. Gonzalez liked the idea, and the Labor Fed entered into a partnership with California DSA and SEIU-UHW (the proponent of Prop 40). In 2012, the California Federation of Teachers (CFT) and a progressive tax coalition organized across the state in an effort that culminated in the passage of a measure that put a tax on the top 2% of income earners in California in order to fund public education and healthcare. This year, voters will decide on whether to make that tax permanent via Prop 3 . It currently generates between $5 to $15 billion annually. If it does not pass, the tax will sunset in 2030, and 1 in 6 public school teachers will be facing layoffs. In response to HR1’s cuts to Medi-Cal, Service Employees International Union - United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), a labor union of over 120,000 healthcare workers across California, advanced a ballot measure, Prop 40 , to create a one time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires, payable either all at once, or via 1% increments over 5 years. This is anticipated to raise about $100 billion and to provide adequate funding to cover the gap in Medi-Cal’s budget wrought by HR1. This tax applies to any billionaires who were residents of the state at the start of 2026, or who will pay state income taxes for the year (at the start of 2026, around 216 billionaires lived in the state; presently, there are around 240). California DSA endorsed both measures earlier this year, and has been coordinating canvasses, phonebanks, and communications in the run up to election day as we work to build a stronger left-labor pole capable of taking on the billionaires. Coming just a week after Bernie Sanders held rallies in San Francisco and Los Angeles to promote Prop 40, the day of action featured multiple local rallies and canvasses in which DSA members joined their local labor councils and union members to spread the class-struggle message that it was high time for the working class to take on the ultra-rich. In the lead up to Tax the Rich Day, Gonzalez blasted out an email, titled “It's time to Tax The Rich!,” in which she promoted events on California DSA’s landing page, and wrote: “I think we can all agree: billionaires have too much damn money. … No matter where you are in California, there is a protest or a canvass event near you this Saturday, October 10, where you can join our fight to tax the rich and pass Prop 3 and Prop 40, and to defeat Prop 41 and Prop 42!” Actions took place that day across 8 cities, including Los Angeles, San Diego, San Jose, the Inland Empire, and the East Bay. The Labor Federation promoted and celebrated them on social media https://bsky.app/profile/californialabor.bsky.social/post/3mxkcazz6422v https://bsky.app/profile/californialabor.bsky.social/post/3mxkco3ub422v https://bsky.app/profile/californialabor.bsky.social/post/3mxkd5m24vk2v https://bsky.app/profile/californialabor.bsky.social/post/3mxmvzfrkbs2v In Hayward, an East Bay city south of Oakland, East Bay DSA joined forces with the Alameda Labor Council for a tax the rich rally and canvass. The Labor Fed posted that “the East Bay did not come to play!” East Bay DSA, since August, has been partnering with the Labor Council to provide volunteers for phone banks and canvasses of the labor council’s 130,000 union members in Alameda County, focused on passing Props 3 and 40 and re-electing DSA-endorsed school board candidates in Oakland. East Bay DSA’s posters, signs and banners, designed by David Solnit and fashioned at an EBDSA art build, have been featured at canvasses, like this one on September 19. Inland Empire DSA heard the call from CA DSA for a Tax the Rich Day on October 10th, and put together a rally in collaboration with SEIU-UHW and PSL at City Hall in downtown Riverside. Over fifty volunteers from Inland Empire DSA, SEIU-UHW, PFP, PSL and Teamsters 1932 as well as Riverside City Councilmember Clarissa Cervantes showed up in support of taxing the state’s billionaires. Volunteer organizers led a march around City Hall and the surrounding area and held a tabling event in front of City Hall to speak to passers-by about how vital passing Proposition 40 (and defeating Propositions 41 and 42!) is to save our healthcare system and provide necessary funding to education and food assistance in the state. Immediately afterward, volunteers headed down to the SEIU-UHW headquarters in downtown Riverside to phone bank for Proposition 40, and IE DSA will be hosting joint phonebanks with SEIU-UHW weekly from now until the election. Angelenos turned out to canvasses in South Central and the Eastside to talk about LA City Council District 9 candidate Estuardo Mazariegos and Congressional District 34 candidate Angela Gonzales Torres alongside the need to pass Prop 40 to redistribute power from billionaires to working people. Later that day, a comedy and karaoke fundraiser capped the night off in support of efforts to tax the rich. California DSA’s statewide working group will be meeting Tuesday, October 20th, at 6pm in order to continue planning and coordinating efforts in support of Props 3 and 40. You can RSVP here: https://www.californiadsa.org/calendar/tax-the-rich-wg-2026oct20 The California Federation of Labor Unions Prop 40 will be hosting a phonebank in support of Prop 40 on October 21st and 5:30pm: https://www.mobilize.us/caaflcio/event/1056391/

articles.title: Two weeks: Time to Overdo it
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: “You can sleep when you’re dead.” —Benjamin Franklin There are just two weeks to go before one of the most consequential elections in the history of California. Driving the existential nature of this election is the onset and growth of the fascist cancer within American capitalism, pushed into metastatic overdrive by the election of Donald Trump to his second term in 2024. In the two years since, he has checked every box in any rational person’s understanding of what the word “fascism” means. As a result we are facing End Times Fascism — the term (and the title of their new book) coined by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor—meaning that this time around, fascists are sucking us down the chutes of climate destruction, democratic devolution, and rapidly eroding institutional means to reverse the tide. While all of DSA’s endorsed election campaigns throughout the state are important and contribute in various ways to the anti-fascist cause, I will go out on a limb to suggest that the campaign that can best serve the anti-fascist struggle is the dual effort to tax the rich via Props 3 and 40. Why? Here we find an unprecedented opportunity—not one, but two tax the rich ballot measures up for a vote in one election. Each is essential to the wellbeing of the working class—one for education, the other for health care. Loss of either would be a disaster and a boon to billionaires. Conversely, passage of both would send an urgently needed message: that the wealth of the rich is not invincible, because an organized working class can be the greater force. Money shores up the power and power shores up the money You recall those two photos of Elon Musk early in 2025: wielding with sick glee a chain saw to demonstrate what his DOGE project was doing to the helping services of the federal government, and his Nazi salute at a MAGA rally? These were accurate signals of an emboldened and newly unified far right sector of capital, melding the formerly antagonistic interests of fossil fuel and big tech, brought together by Trump to supercharge the development of AI and its evil twin, data centers, under the control of corporations. The combined resources of these two capital sectors united in support of the fascist program is the reason why political spending hit record levels in the 2024 elections, and why it is on track to break the record again this year. As Klein and Taylor make clear, mix hitherto undreamed of quantities of capital with Christian nationalism, perpetual war in the Middle East fanning the flames of religious fantasy along with the climate crisis, reckless investment in AI, the Trump administration’s removal of all federal regulatory controls, and you have the perfect cocktail for apocalypse. The richest people in the world think they can escape the dystopia they are consciously unleashing—to island bunkers, to the Rapture, to outer space—as they run the rest of us over the cliff and the earth to the end of its tether. Here in California the billionaires’ push to defeat Prop 40 will set new spending records for ballot initiatives. That’s pocket change from their bloated portfolios. The campaign to pass Props 3 and 40 directly challenges the fascist program, valuing human need over uncontrolled profitmaking, saying yes to life and to the earth, and reducing the purses of the superrich and thus their power. If we win, we demonstrate that the power of people can outweigh the power of money. Time to Overdo it I’m asking everyone who reads these words to add just a bit of work—something, anything— to election work you are already doing in the next two weeks to help get Props 3 and 40 passed. I’m not arguing that anyone should stop their campaigning for a local city council candidate or US congressional seat and replace that work with the Prop 3 and 40 tax the rich campaign between now and November 3. I’m saying something else, and I admit it runs against the grain of the advice that a lifetime of activist labor and socialist politics has led me to consistently offer comrades and other activists, which is, “Don’t overdo it.” Passion for political causes can easily tip over into burnout, which is not helpful for the long run. But we are up against an enemy that is literally attempting to destroy the long run. And so I make an exception this time so that it’s not the last time. In other words, for the next two weeks, let’s overdo it. Our final California DSA Tax the Rich Working Group meeting of the campaign is this Tuesday night at 6 pm; join us to hear what we’re planning . You could also join the Prop 40 phone bank on 10/21 at 5:30 . Here is tonight’s Prop 3 phone bank link . It can also be simpler. You can grab a posterboard from an art supply store and make your own sign for Yes on 3, Yes on 40, Tax the Rich and stand on a street corner with a friend or two. You can put a sign up in your window. You can call your friends and tell them to vote yes on 3 and 40 and no on 41, 42, and 43. You can download flyers and pass them out in your workplace. With your help taxing the rich is possible. Once we’ve done that we can rest (contra Franklin, we don’t have to wait til we’re dead) recover from burnout, and breathe the air of a world slightly less imperiled by fascism.

articles.title: The Midterms May Be America’s Last Best Chance to Stop End Times Fascism
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: “The new lords of the global village are not just Wall Street insiders or run-of-the-mill plutocrats; they are a disparate, distinctly more anarchic group of powerful forces.” Just in time for the midterms, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor have delivered an incredibly relevant new book, End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World , that quite plainly lays out what is at stake in the coming election. We are living under a new form of authoritarianism that has already deeply weakened our democracy and threatens to push us over the cliff toward a dystopian future where only our new oligarchs will be able to survive the harsh social, economic, and environmental realities we face. Klein and Taylor survey the landscape of contemporary analyses of authoritarianism and name the present system “End Times Fascism,” a unique strain of political disease that has flourished due to several factors that have emerged out of the circumstances of our current Gilded Age. What characterizes the malady that afflicts us? In sum, we are ruled by a nearly totally unaccountable elite. As they note: At its core, end times fascism is a crisis of rampant impunity born of concentrated power and wealth. Far too much money, information technology, and weaponry have been allowed to concentrate into the hands of the few, and that unchecked power has deranged our elites, goading them to take risks that put our societies and countless species at risk. And if the risks taken by contemporary elites seem to be crossing lines that other members of the traditional oligarchy were loath to trespass, that’s because they are. The new lords of the global village are not just Wall Street insiders or run-of-the-mill plutocrats; they are a disparate, distinctly more anarchic group of powerful forces. End times fascism is not the product of a coherent movement: “rather than a monolith, it is an alliance of very different groups, each one racing toward a different but related apocalyptic dream, sutured together in common cause . . . religious end timers, the tech end timers, and the ethno-nationalist end timers.” Hence the ongoing barrage of assaults on everything from education, civil rights, and freedom of speech to environmental sustainability and democratic institutions of all kinds seems like an unfocused shotgun blast because it is coming from several different angles all at once. Rushing towards climate catastrophe, unchecked oligarchy, and patriarchal, white supremacist retrenchment as the AI onslaught undermines our sense of reality and ability to think critically is only possible because the chaos creates polycrises and a blitzkrieg of disruptions makes it hard for the average person to get a clear cognitive map of power. And the resulting radical uncertainty unmoors people from their traditional bearings and allows the end times fascists to portray themselves as our saviors from the very threats that they have unleashed on the world. We might not survive them, but they don’t care. Their end game is not to save anything but themselves. As Klein and Taylor argue: [F]ascist movements claim to be defending powerful institutions—the nation, the market, the military, the family—from internal and external pollutants. In the logic of fascism, the task of defeating those threats and reimposing order, requires emergency measures, often destroying many of the very institutions fascists claim to be defending. Enter Trump and company as they prepare to contest what is looking like a tsunami of Democratic voters this November. The huge margins they will likely lose by in most places have made their task harder, but this has not deterred them. After discovering that their initial attempts to interfere with the midterms would not bear fruit, the MAGA right has simply found new roads to the ruin of American democracy. Seymour Hersch outlines their most likely next move on his Substack: So here comes the GOP’s Plan B, which still depends on election deniers who have been voted into office in states with contested Senate seats that could decide the fate of Trump’s last two years in office. I was told that the targets, in terms of putting election deniers to work, are now limited to five states where a few thousand votes could make the difference in the political makeup of the Senate: Ohio, Texas, Alaska, Iowa, and Kansas. The election counting machinery in each state is now in the control of elected Republican voting officials who are Trump supporters. In two other states, Georgia and North Carolina, Republican candidates are in trouble and Democratic candidates are comfortably ahead in polling. “If the election is close,” one insider explained to me, “you would only have to disqualify as few as seven thousand voters” in primarily Democratic precincts “to change the outcome.” One thought now, I was told, is to call on election deniers in the toss-up states to find ways to use existing federal data, verified or not, to challenge thousands of votes in key Democratic precincts. (Trump said yesterday that he would not rule out invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, if he deems it necessary. Let us call that Plan C.) Hence, it would not be wise to let the ugly polls for the GOP make us complacent or allow Trump’s increasingly pathetic public persona to lead us to underestimate the danger we face. In sum, the crazier Trump seems, the more likely it is that he may just try to do the previously unthinkable and bring more troops back onto American streets. His Triumph of the Will style taxpayer funded TV ads are signaling how he will portray himself as a defender of American institutions as he blithely destroys them. Trump is the very embodiment of an end times fascist. As Klein and Taylor argue, “We should believe our eyes. The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating.” Vote and be vigilant, dear reader. The end times fascists will not go gently into their good night. Indeed, even if we are successful in pushing back against the tide of authoritarianism in the midterms, so much more remains to be done. Klein and Taylor note that the task at hand will require us commit to the continuous work of occupying and defending the “paradise” of the “here” and “now.” Following Walter Benjamin, they call for a “messianism of the here and now” that is best embodied at present by the movement, with DSA at its center, that brought Zohran Mamdani to power in New York. Mamdani’s campaign does not give us the perfect answer, but it does show us some of the rules of the road: There is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism; every front will take on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and the Mamdani campaign embodied many of them. Start from love of place; conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives: embrace common goals across difference; get outside and gather offline and in person; take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul. We need to build a world where we start to see “the word neighbor growing to expand to include thousands of people we have never met and who have yet to arrive.” More than anything else, Klein and Taylor suggest, we need to never lose sight of either what we are fighting against nor what the future we want should look like. This article first appeared in The Jumping Off Place

articles.title: How Revolutionary, Really, Was Christianity?
articles.author: Molly Judd
articles.content: In the Acts of the Apostles, the followers of Jesus Christ are repeatedly described as belonging to “the Way.” In the modern Christian lexicon, this phrase is often understood as a spiritual path rather than a physical one. One travels the Way from a life without Christ to one with him. Returning to the original ancient Greek texts, the classicist Tim Whitmarsh points out that the word that underpins the idea of the Way, hodos , can mean a spiritual path, but it can also, and more often, means a physical road — or a journey along one. Paul and other early Christian missionaries were on a spiritual journey, but they were also on what Whitmarsh calls a literal road trip, traveling across modern-day Turkey, Syria, Greece, and elsewhere to convert anyone who would listen. They made these journeys through a Roman world whose network of roads had been dramatically reorganized and extended under Augustus, facilitating movement across the empire. Whitmarsh’s new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity , asks how revolutionary the religion really was, and does so by situating its original texts in the context from which they emerged and which aided their success: the Roman Empire, and the myriad cultures that it encompassed. The question of Christianity’s influence is usually fought out at the extremes. On one side are the New Atheists of the 2000s, among them the late Christopher Hitchens ( God Is Not Great ) and Richard Dawkins ( The God Delusion ), who saw religion as a poison to be reasoned out of existence. On the other are the likes of Tom Holland, whose Dominion argues that Christianity broke with the ancient world and shaped the West’s ideas of morality, compassion and human dignity — arguments he has carried to a vast audience through The Rest Is History podcast. Whitmarsh does something neither camp can. He does not argue against Christian belief; he argues against Christian uniqueness, and his tool is philology rather than polemic. Reading the texts in their original languages, he shows that much of what seems distinctive about the Christian narrative stems from cultural tropes already circulating in the Roman Empire and that it spread along the infrastructure the empire provided. Because he finds the revolution in Rome rather than in the church, he comes close to dismantling Holland’s thesis that Christianity was revolutionary, without having to debunk the faith: if roads, languages and the constant movement of people made Christianity possible, then it was the empire, not the new religion, that remade the world. He is not anti-Christian so much as anti-exceptionalist. He develops this through two concepts. The first is what he calls “swirl,” the unprecedented movement of people, goods, and ideas across the empire, which allowed a religion drawing on Jewish, Greek, and Roman culture to flourish. “Paradox” is the idea that the Roman order, stretched across such vast territories, tended to provoke its opposite, as it did in the birth of Christianity. Swirl is where Whitmarsh is at his best, his grip on ancient languages taking him back to original sources. A Boy Is Born Roughly two thousand years ago, a biographer told of a boy whose birth was preceded by a portent announcing that nature was pregnant with a king, after which the city’s leaders, fearful of losing power, ordered that all new male offspring be killed. You’d be forgiven for thinking this is the story of the birth of Jesus, so close to the slaughter of the innocents ordered by Herod. In fact, this account comes not from the Gospels but from Suetonius — and the boy in question was Augustus. We find similar accounts in the poetry of the time. Virgil’s Fourth Eclogue , composed around 40 BCE, prophesies a golden age ushered in by the birth of a boy, arriving when virgo (the “virgin,” evoking Astraea, goddess of justice) returns. Whitmarsh doesn’t propose a direct line from Virgil to the Gospels; rather, he suggests the poem may be one strand in a wider swirl of savior-birth imagery circulating in the Roman world — imagery that Christian writers would later draw on independently. More speculatively, he traces the poem’s own birth narrative back further still to the birth stories of Alexander the Great and to Jewish scripture. In Jewish scripture, Isaiah predicts that a time of prospering will be preempted by a sign, when a woman will conceive and bear a son named Emmanuel (7:14). Returning to the original Hebrew, Whitmarsh points out that the word used to describe the woman is almah , which generally means a young woman of childbearing age rather than specifically a virgin. In the Greek Old Testament, this was translated as parthenos , a word whose range of meanings includes “virgin” — and which Matthew later uses when quoting Isaiah in his account of Jesus’s birth. Whitmarsh takes this a step further, asking whether Virgil (who could read Greek) may have encountered versions of this Jewish tradition as well as narratives of Alexander the Great’s birth. Drawing these threads together, Whitmarsh suggests that the Christian story of the virgin birth emerged partly through this movement between languages: Jewish scripture translated into Greek, reinterpreted by Christian writers, and read against the same swirling Greek-speaking culture that Virgil himself inhabited. On this reading, Virgil and Matthew are less cause and effect than two writers independently reaching into the same pool of Greek-Jewish material — Virgil’s virgo , already carrying the multiple meanings of Astraea and justice, potentially absorbing yet another resonance in the process. It is an arresting example of his swirl in action. Imaginative Spaces Whitmarsh is on firm ground when dealing with language and translations, but his arguments feel somewhat shakier when he turns to larger hypotheses. He proposes that Augustan dominance of both the physical and political spheres provoked a counterreaction in the form of a seeking out of alternative imaginative spaces. Noting the tendency of Greek literature of the second century to look up or down to venture into new spaces — whether in the form of narratives concerned with deep-sea diving or trips to the moon — Whitmarsh argues that this fascination with finding new spaces beyond governmental control extended to the first Christians too. Early Christian literature conveys a powerful sense of space and travel — whether Paul’s journeying in Acts or the Gospels’ descriptions of distant and unfamiliar places. In time, it would be the desert that would dominate the setting of the Christian imagination in the Life of Anthony . It is here, though, that Whitmarsh’s textual precision gives way to something looser. For instance, the claim that a whole imaginative geography, from lunar voyages to the desert fathers, can be read as a counterreaction to Augustan order is suggested rather than demonstrated; Rome’s Age of Revolution asks the reader to accept a fair amount of inference, in a book otherwise so careful to show its working. Paradox, unlike swirl, is a harder idea to ground in the sources. A Novel Approach In the final sections of the book, Whitmarsh moves away from a focus on Augustus and his revolutions and toward a dissection of the Greek-speaking culture of the eastern empire and its role as an incubator of early Christianity. It is here that he lands his biggest argumentative punches, showing both swirl and paradox at work. He takes aim at the “Hollywood image” of persistent, structural opposition between Christians and Romans. Executions and persecution certainly happened, he explains, but martyrdom stories exaggerated and dramatized them, and they did so using narrative forms borrowed from the newly emerging genre of the Greek novel. Take the martyrdom tale The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity , which tells of the arrest and public killing of the young noblewoman Perpetua, still nursing her infant, and her fellow Christian Felicity, who gave birth shortly before their execution, in 203 CE. Crucially, the text was produced in a world in which Christianity was not subject to a straightforward empire-wide ban. A stable Roman order, paradoxically, gave Christians the space to write up stories of persecution and for these tales to flourish. Whitmarsh argues, against those who read the story as eyewitness testimony, that it relies on strategies borrowed from the Greek novel: pity, tension, and, most of all, eroticism. In the arena, he notes, the women are stripped and put in nets, and the crowd recoils at the sight of Perpetua’s lactating breasts. They are then thrown to a “ferocious cow,” an animal chosen, the text tells us, to match their sex. Perpetua is tossed by the cow, and she is forced to rearrange her clothing to cover her thighs. Later the crowd demands that the martyrs be brought into the center of the arena, so that “they might join their eyes with the sword that penetrated their bodies.” The text is laced with innuendo and sexual imagery, drawing the reader in and allowing them to enjoy it under the alibi of a dedication to Christian martyrdom. Notes on the Visual The Greek novel is Whitmarsh’s final argumentative device, and though successful, as an art historian I am left wondering if he has neglected the visual culture in which early Christianity was operating. Rome’s Age of Revolution is primarily concerned with textual analysis, though if it does have a visual signature, it’s the cover: a detail from a Roman mosaic of Dionysus, found in a Roman villa excavated at Corinth. It’s a striking choice — the kaleidoscopic mosaic tiles presenting a literal manifestation of the swirl of which Whitmarsh writes. The content of the mosaic speaks directly to Whitmarsh’s argument: Corinth was a Greek city remade under the Roman Empire, and Dionysus was a Greek god displayed here within a Roman urban setting. Whitmarsh shows (without referencing the cover) that several pagan texts, even those written as late as the second century CE, align Dionysus with Jesus: he had a divine father and mortal mother, could turn water into wine, performed supernatural wonders, and died before coming back to life. But beyond the cover and a few brief mentions of material culture in the book, Whitmarsh excludes this visual line of enquiry. This is understandable, given he is not an art historian, but there are many times when a brief interlude may have added to his argument. On a recent trip to Rome, a label in the Vatican Museums taught me that the Good Shepherd motif so central to early Christian iconography was modeled on the kriophoros , or ram-bearer, a figure already centuries old in Greek art and closely associated with the god Hermes. The label went further, suggesting Christians adopted this borrowed imagery partly because its familiarity let them worship somewhat covertly under Roman eyes — the same shepherd could read as Hermes to a suspicious neighbor and as Christ to a fellow believer. It’s a tidy story but I found myself doubting it, and Whitmarsh’s dismantling of the Hollywood image of relentless persecution gave me reason to look deeper. Many scholars of early Christian art are now cautious about treating such imagery primarily as a form of disguise: Christians may instead have been adapting a visual language their neighbors already knew how to read, recasting an image associated with care and safe passage within a new theology, rather than smuggling one past the authorities. If that’s right, the Good Shepherd isn’t evidence of a persecuted religion in hiding — it’s another instance of exactly the kind of confident, opportunistic repurposing that Whitmarsh traces through Christian texts. Whitmarsh gives us a masterclass in tracing swirl through language, translation, and narrative and a more tentative case for paradox. But the book’s real achievement is to ask how revolutionary Christianity was without taking either of the usual sides. Christianity, he shows, can be taken seriously as a historical force without being treated as an exception to history. The mosaic on the cover makes the point better than any argument: like the empire itself, it is assembled from borrowed pieces and is no less striking for it. It repays close looking, and so does this book. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
