articles.title: End of the Melting Pot
articles.author: Javier A. Hernandez
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The most significant demographic shift happening in the U.S. is not just the rise of a Hispanic minority, but the creation of a lasting, multicultural Hispanic-American community spanning various states and metro areas. This community is supported by millions of people, trillions in economic activity, a growing voter base, established Spanish-language institutions, and ongoing cultural ties to Latin America and Spain. While English remains the dominant language nationwide and language assimilation persists over generations, the large scale of Hispanic America shows that integration no longer means cultural loss. Instead, Hispanics are both becoming more American and enriching the U.S. with Hispanic culture. The figures are remarkable. In 2024, the Hispanic population reached around 68 million, making up approximately 20 percent of the U.S. population. Hispanics contributed nearly 71 percent to the total population growth between 2022 and 2023, mainly due to births and immigration. By 2024, 79 percent of U.S. Latinos were American citizens, with approximately two-thirds being citizens by birth. This shift shows that Hispanic influence in the United States is no longer just about newcomers arriving; it now involves millions of American citizens actively transforming American culture in both appearance and sound. Hispanic America Is Older Than the United States The traditional view of immigration often overlooks an important point: Hispanic civilization in North America predates 20th-century immigration. Spain founded St. Augustine, Florida, in 1565, over forty years before Jamestown. Spanish exploration and settlements stretched across Florida, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. According to the Library of Congress, Spain governed much of the present-day American Southwest from 1598 to 1821, and Spanish missions, presidios, towns, roads, and ranching communities created cultural landscapes that persisted beyond the periods of Mexican and American control. Modern Hispanic growth can be seen as both a result of immigration and a re-emergence of an established Hispanic North American culture. Cities like Los Angeles, San Antonio, Santa Fe, San Diego, and El Paso, among many others, show that Hispanic influence is not an external addition to North American history but part of it. What has changed is the extent of this presence. Related: Puerto Rico Doesn’t Need to Beg Congress for Citizenship. It Needs Sovereignty. The Emergence of a Hispanic Cultural Region Hispanic America is not a single contiguous region and is not culturally uniform. It includes diverse communities such as Mexicans, Puerto Ricans, Cubans, Dominicans, Salvadorans, Colombians, Venezuelans, Spaniards, among others, each with unique national histories and identities. The federal definition of Hispanic includes individuals with Mexican, Puerto Rican, Cuban, Central or South American, or Spanish cultural backgrounds. However, these populations are gradually creating what can be described as a Hispanic Cultural Region : a connected geographical and institutional area where factors such as population density, Spanish-language use, commerce, education, media, political engagement, and transnational networks enable Hispanic culture to sustain and reproduce itself. It looks more like an archipelago than a single territory. One hub includes California, Arizona, New Mexico, Nevada, Colorado, and Texas, all former Mexican territories and previously part of New Spain. Another focuses on Florida and its large Caribbean and Latin American communities. A northeastern corridor runs from metropolitan Washington through New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts. Chicago serves as a key center of Mexican and Puerto Rican cultures and peoples, while Hispanic populations are growing in Georgia, North Carolina, and other Southern states. Within this large cultural area, Miami comfortably operates in both Spanish and English. Spanish is prevalent in daily commerce in Los Angeles, San Antonio, and El Paso. Throughout New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, neighborhoods are influenced by the Puerto Rican, Cuban, Mexican, and Dominican communities. Connecticut and Massachusetts both have large Hispanic populations, especially Puerto Ricans. Although these regions are definitively part of the United States, they also culturally engage with a broader transnational Hispanic community, participating in both American and Hispanic worlds. Spanish and the Limits of Assimilation Language serves as perhaps the clearest indicator of this resilience. Spanish remains the dominant non-English language nationwide. Census data indicates that approximately 62 percent of Americans who speak a language other than English at home speak Spanish. Within Hispanic communities, 68 percent still speak Spanish at home as of 2024. Pew Research shows that around 75 percent of Latino adults can hold a conversation in Spanish effectively. Assimilation definitely occurs, but not in the manner many Americans want or agree with. As generations pass, English skills improve, and Spanish usage decreases among some people, but not all. However, this does not automatically end the culture. Spanish has unique strengths that most immigrant languages once lacked: millions of speakers within the country, regional concentration, ongoing connections with Latin America, widespread Spanish TV and digital content, international cultural scenes, bilingual businesses, universities, churches, schools, and ongoing migration. The outcome might not be full linguistic separation or total assimilation, but the slow development of a continental bilingual Hispanic cultural system in which English remains the national lingua franca, while Spanish becomes more institutionalized, important, and ubiquitous in key regions and major urban centers. Education plays a crucial role in this process. Among English learners in American schools, Spanish remains the predominant home language, and dual-language programs are increasingly viewing bilingualism as an educational asset rather than just remediation. Related: Puerto Rico’s Streets Are Erupting Again: Washington Should Pay Attention From Demographic Weight to Economic and Political Power The cultural shift is supported by significant economic strength. UCLA researchers estimated that the U.S. Latino economy generated about $4.4 trillion in 2024. If considered as a separate economy, it would be among the world’s largest. They also found that real Latino economic output increased by 6.4 percent in 2024, outpacing non-Latino growth. Demography is increasingly translated into political influence. In 2024, around 36.2 million Hispanics were eligible to vote, accounting for 14.7 percent of the electorate, up from just 14.3 million eligible Hispanic voters in 2000. This does not create a unified Hispanic political bloc. In fact, nearly fifty percent of Hispanic voters backed Donald Trump in 2024. This political diversity reflects institutional growth: Hispanic voters are becoming a key electorate that both parties need to compete for, rather than being a predictable and peripheral group. A Growing Cultural Cleavage Demographic changes have also led to political pushback. In March 2025, President Trump declared English the official language of the United States. While the order does not ban Spanish-language government services, it reflects a wider political trend favoring linguistic assimilation. A more extreme perspective is seen in the “Great Replacement” arguments, which claim that immigration is deliberately used to substitute the country’s traditionally white population. The Anti-Defamation League traces the origins of this theory to white-nationalist movements, while recent studies show how variations of this rhetoric have gained traction among elite political circles. It is important to note that not all conservatives or supporters of stricter immigration policies endorse this ideology. Still, its increasing prominence highlights how some Americans interpret demographic shifts as cultural threats rather than natural social changes. The Trump administration’s tougher immigration enforcement introduces new concerns. ICE reports higher removals, raids, and arrests. A 2025 Pew survey revealed that 52% of Latino adults worry about deportation for themselves or loved ones, and 59% have seen or heard of recent enforcement actions in their communities. Importantly, this anxiety affects not only unauthorized immigrants but also citizen families and mixed-status communities. The emerging divide is not just between Republican and Democrat, or immigrant and native-born. Instead, it revolves around differing views of American identity: one focusing on linguistic and cultural unity and assimilation centered on an English-speaking American national identity, and the other becoming more accepting of lasting bilingualism, multicultural backgrounds, and complex identities. Related: The Psychology of Empire: Colonialism, Race, and the Battle for Puerto Rico’s Mind Puerto Rican Identity and Cultural Resistance Puerto Ricans serve as an illustrative example because American citizenship has not diminished Puerto Rican national identity, culture, and resistance to U.S. colonialism and assimilation policies. Recent political and cultural developments reveal a significant interest in national sovereignty and independence among younger Puerto Ricans. In the 2024 gubernatorial election, Juan Dalmau, representing the Puerto Rican Independence Party and Citizen Victory Movement alliance, secured a historic second-place finish. By 2026, journalists documented a rising youth-led independence movement with active organizations within Puerto Rico and diaspora communities like New York. In fact, a growing movement among Puerto Ricans supports Puerto Rico’s reunification with Spain as an autonomous community within the Spanish state, celebrating their Hispanidad. Some younger diaspora Puerto Rican activists highlight that, although they grew up in the United States, their Puerto Rican identity stays strong through speaking Spanish, enjoying music, supporting independence, and embracing their nationality. This shows that living in the U.S. does not necessarily weaken their connection to their Hispanic and Puerto Rican roots. For many Puerto Ricans, resisting American assimilation (both historically and personally) is a point of pride. Puerto Rican national identity can encompass citizenship, nationality, culture, and a sense of diaspora all at once. Spain and Hispanidad Hispanic America is becoming more connected to a global Spanish-speaking cultural network. Spain actively promotes Spanish language and culture in the U.S. through the Instituto Cervantes , educational diplomacy, and the Spanish Embassy’s Education Office. Cervantes runs American centers and programs in cities like New York, Chicago, Albuquerque, and El Paso, providing language classes, cultural activities, and professional development - including programs tailored for heritage Spanish speakers. Spain’s Education Office clarifies its mission as promoting collaborative educational initiatives between Spain and the United States and establishing enduring links between their people. It also works with Spanish universities to prepare American teachers of Spanish. These connections situate Hispanic Americans within Hispanidad, a transatlantic community that shares language and culture and includes Latin America, Spain, and other Hispanic groups worldwide. Related: The Farce of “Economic Freedom” in Puerto Rico The Hispanization of North America The United States is unlikely to stop being primarily English-speaking anytime soon, but Spanish is already the country’s de facto second language. Hispanics are also not immune to assimilation. However, these facts do not negate the broader shift. The country is evolving from a society where immigrant cultures were expected to fade away into an English-speaking American mainstream (the famous “melting pot”), toward a more bilingual cultural landscape across the continent. In this new cultural system, a large Hispanic population can thrive and maintain a unique identity indefinitely, supported by demographics, economic influence, geographic concentration, political representation, and international cultural ties. This captures the deeper significance of Hispanic America: it’s not just an immigrant community adopting an American identity, but a diverse, multinational Hispanic population reshaping what America truly means. The emerging Hispanic Cultural Region does not need borders, autonomy, or political separation to exist. Its foundation comprises families, neighborhoods, schools, businesses, churches, Spanish-language media, music, political groups, and digital networks linking cities like Los Angeles to Mexico City, Miami to Havana and Caracas, New York to San Juan and Santo Domingo, and Hispanic communities across the country to Madrid and the broader Spanish-speaking world. As a result, America’s future might lie beyond mere assimilation or cultural division. This represents a new historical phenomenon: a United States that is becoming more bilingual and Hispanicized, where millions actively participate in American civic life while choosing not to see the abandonment of Spanish, ancestral roots, and Hispanic culture as the cost of their inclusion.

articles.title: Tenant Displacement
articles.author: Jack Ross
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Behind every door was a chance to make money. It was 2020, and Matt DeBoth and Angel Escobar were canvassing Koreatown, Highland Park and other gentrifying Los Angeles neighborhoods, trying to get tenants, mostly working-class immigrants, to give up some of the city’s most affordable apartments. Each time a tenant agreed, DeBoth later said in a deposition, he and Escobar could get a bonus of up to $1,000. They worked for K3 Holdings LLC, a landlord based in Beverly Hills, California, which was rapidly acquiring dozens of rent-controlled properties across L.A. The company’s plan was to pay the longtime tenants to leave their homes — usually tens of thousands of dollars — and then raise the rent substantially for the next occupants, according to internal K3 records reviewed by Capital & Main. In spreadsheets, DeBoth and Escobar tracked tenants’ rent — and how much K3 could likely increase it if they left. A “notes” column recorded the company’s progress: “Roof collapsed- extremely obese man and sister… should be an easy buyout.” “Recently diagnosed with cancer, so he’s saying no at the moment.” “Matt got tenant to move out for free by telling him lease was expired.” The spreadsheets and other K3 records were among a trove of internal emails, reports and other company documents produced through discovery in a 2022 federal housing discrimination lawsuit filed against K3 and its affiliates by 16 low-income tenants who alleged the company “targeted” them as Latinos. The records offer a rare, inside look at how a large landlord executed a “cash for keys” operation, a widespread strategy that has reshaped gentrifying neighborhoods across California as the state grapples with a severe housing crisis. Landlords continue to favor the strategy because it is one of the fastest ways to dramatically increase the value of a real estate investment. Cash for keys deals — in which landlords pay tenants to vacate their apartments without being evicted — are legal as long as they are voluntary agreements. But if a landlord uses deception or coercive tactics to pressure tenants into signing, the deals can be illegal under L.A.’s Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance. The documents produced through discovery for the federal case also show K3 employees writing about ways to get tenants to leave their units without paying them and discussing what DeBoth described as “the narrative” that their buildings — which are standing and occupied today — would be demolished. Using “intentional misrepresentation” to persuade tenants to relinquish their leases is prohibited under the city’s ordinance. K3 Holdings was founded by Nathan Kadisha and Michael Kadisha, well-connected twin brothers in their early thirties who have positioned themselves as affordable housing champions. They are the nephews of billionaire Neil Kadisha, who co-founded Omninet Capital , a real estate investment firm that has acquired roughly 13,000 residential rental units and about 9 million square feet of commercial space across 11 states. The Kadishas established K3 in 2016 and purchased 36 rent-controlled properties in just seven years, according to a report from the city’s Housing Department. Between 2018 and 2023, they acquired nearly 900 rent-stabilized units, making K3 Holdings the fastest-growing owner of rent-controlled apartments in Los Angeles during that period, the report said. Landlords have used cash for keys-style buyouts for decades in Los Angeles and in other cities with rent control, such as New York . But according to a Capital & Main analysis of city data, the Kadishas stand out for the scale and pace at which they executed the strategy in Los Angeles, when K3 bought out hundreds of tenants in just a few years and replaced them with higher-paying renters. Tenant plaintiffs and activists with the Los Angeles Tenants Union, which organized renters in dozens of K3 properties, said K3 was only able to work that quickly by illegally harassing tenants into moving out. Under California’s Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act , if a tenant vacates a rent-controlled apartment, the owner is allowed to raise the unit’s rent to market rates, setting a new benchmark for future regulated increases. And that can easily amount to many hundreds of dollars or more each month for a single apartment. This story is based largely on records from the 2022 federal lawsuit that were temporarily misclassified as nonconfidential and released publicly in 2023. Capital & Main sent detailed questions to K3 founder and principal Nathan Kadisha. The company responded through attorney Oren A. Lazar, who, in a five-page letter, denied allegations of tenant harassment and threatened to sue for defamation. Those allegations “were litigated by capable plaintiffs’ counsel for nearly two years in federal court. No court ever found K3 or the Kadishas liable for any of them. K3 denied those allegations then, publicly and consistently, and denies them now,” he wrote. Related: Remodeled Shipping Containers—‘LA style’: Solution for America’s Affordable Housing Shortage? Threatened With Deportation According to documents produced through discovery for the federal lawsuit, to persuade residents to vacate, K3 Holdings deployed DeBoth, the company’s asset manager, and Escobar, an employee described by tenants in interviews as a young man who sometimes used a pseudonym — and whose temper flared when residents refused his money. Three current or former K3 tenants told Capital & Main that Escobar or other company employees threatened them with deportation after they didn’t sign buyout agreements, an allegation DeBoth called “absolutely bullshit” when tenant attorneys deposed him in the eviction lawsuits. (Two of those allegations were made in 2022; the third was in 2026.) DeBoth declined to respond to questions from Capital & Main through his lawyer, Ranojoy Guha. Escobar — who no longer works for K3 Holdings — also declined to respond to questions when reached by phone. “I have nothing to say,” Escobar said. K3, through its attorney, denied that employees “threatened tenants with deportation or other immigration consequences.” In the federal housing discrimination lawsuit, tenants also alleged that K3 employed a variety of illegal tactics to coerce them into taking cash payouts, including threatening them with eviction, failing to provide them with Spanish language documents, and allowing conditions to deteriorate so that the aging buildings were simply too miserable to live in. They accused the company of “targeting Latinx families” with its buyouts, then renovating their empty units and advertising them to a “whiter” and “younger” clientele. K3 settled the federal housing discrimination lawsuit in 2023 for $2.2 million and assurances that it would take numerous actions to encourage a diverse tenant base. The company did not acknowledge any wrongdoing. But in a separate lawsuit scheduled for trial Nov. 2, tenants in a Koreatown property accused K3 of violating state and city housing laws. Among the laws K3 is accused of violating is the Los Angeles Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance , which bars the city’s landlords from threatening tenants with deportation, refusing repairs and maintenance, tricking them into leaving and more. ‘We Are Responsive’ For years, K3 tenants have protested unsafe living conditions in its properties , citing mold outbreaks and rodent and insect infestations they said resulted from poor building maintenance. They also said the company’s aggressive remodels left apartment units vulnerable to flooding. In an email in the documents produced through discovery, a K3 employee said renovations of an empty unit led to flooding of an occupied apartment on the floor below. “Can we manage to hold off on telling [the tenant] that this was caused by an outside vendor during a unit turn if they don’t already know?” director of property management Rita Qatami said in the 2022 email. “I don’t want them to say anything to the tenant union.” K3, through its attorney, denied that it “deliberately neglected its properties to coerce buyouts.” “We’re responsive,” asset manager DeBoth said in his deposition in the 2023 eviction cases. “We are well staffed. We are appropriate.” DeBoth left the company later that year. In 2025, he filed his own lawsuit against K3 Holdings and the Kadishas that accused the company of “systematically failing” to address an “alarming number” of tenant complaints, conducting unpermitted construction and potentially exposing him to “mold, asbestos, lead, or other deadly substances.” In interviews, several tenants said the buyouts were initially tempting — but they quickly learned that the below-market amounts they’d been paying for years in their rent-controlled apartments were impossible to replicate in the city’s stratospheric rental market. Accepting the cash would leave them in even worse financial shape, they said. Related: How Wealthy Neighborhoods Keep New Housing Out “In my country, I had never seen that kind of money,” said Ester Castro, a former K3 tenant from Guatemala who accepted a $30,000 buyout to leave the studio apartment she shared with her two children and who spoke to Capital & Main in Spanish through an interpreter. “You might have this idea that it’s going to last long, that you can use it to build something better or find a better apartment. But you realize that is an illusion,” Castro said. The family now lives in Georgia. K3’s wide-ranging buyout campaign triggered a similarly wide-ranging response from its residents, who formed a tenant union that spanned nearly 40 of K3’s buildings and involved dozens of volunteer organizers at its peak. Under the umbrella of the Los Angeles Tenants Union, the K3 Tenant Council successfully prevented some of the buyouts in the K3 buildings where they organized, creating hubs of tenant power in those properties that endure to this day. For some tenants, the union arrived too late. Organizers described knocking on doors in nearly empty properties where immigrant families had recently lived but hastily vacated, some of them leaving their belongings still piled on the street outside. K3 tenants who accepted buyouts hastily vacate a Koreatown building in the winter of 2023. Photo by Barbara Davidson for Capital & Main. Buyouts at Scale K3 Holdings stands out in city data for the scale and pace with which it pursued tenant buyouts in recent years. Between January 2019 and July 2025, Los Angeles landlords spent more than $148 million on nearly 6,000 cash for keys buyouts, according to data analyzed by L.A. City Controller Kenneth Mejia. A Capital & Main analysis of Mejia’s data found that K3 Holdings completed the most buyouts of any landlord in the city during that time period. Of the top 20 buildings where landlords reported the most buyouts to the Los Angeles Housing Department, nine belonged to K3 Holdings. (The landlord in second place, Yaacov Brenenson of Moriah Capital, owned three properties.) K3’s tally is likely an undercount. At least one K3 property in Koreatown, where the company recorded completing 51 buyouts in its own spreadsheets, is missing from the city data. Sharon Sandow, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Housing Department, confirmed in an email that K3 did not report completing any buyouts at that address. Through its attorney, K3 denied that it concealed buyouts from the city. In the now-settled federal housing discrimination lawsuit, tenants alleged that in pursuing its “gentrification strategy,” K3 set out to target “L.A’s most vulnerable tenants for displacement” in communities “where the racial turnover of tenants generates the most profits with the least resistance.” The discovery documents produced in the federal housing discrimination lawsuit reviewed by Capital & Main showed that K3 was laser-focused on getting tenants to take buyouts. Any tenant paying at least $250 below market rate was typically offered a buyout, DeBoth said in his deposition, adding that company agents won bonuses each time they persuaded a tenant to leave. And chief among the records are three spreadsheets the company used to keep track of the tenants it was prioritizing for buyouts — tenants who paid the lowest rents in the portfolio, whose apartments could be flipped to market rate for the greatest profit. In those spreadsheets, K3 often tallied a success rate based on how many units it had emptied. In one spreadsheet, the company reported a 75% success rate in 33 properties where it bought out 545 units. If rerented at market rate, that could amount to more than $126,000 in new monthly rental income, the document said. In a court filing from the same lawsuit, plaintiffs alleged that the company typically remodeled the units after buying out the old tenants, advertising them online as renovated “fun and fresh” apartments that were close to “restaurants, and nightlife.” Tenants also argued that the company violated federal law against housing segregation by advertising properties “online and only in English” — with some listings allegedly stating that the contact for the property spoke only English. The Demolition ‘Narrative’ The lawsuit brought by Koreatown tenants alleged that DeBoth “tried to coerce tenants into vacating” their apartments by telling them their leases were up, which it described as an “intentional and fraudulent” misrepresentation. And in the internal company documents that were produced as part of the federal housing discrimination lawsuit, K3 employees appeared to write about such attempts. In a November 2021 email to Johanna Gonzalez — then an administrative assistant with the company, according to the document — DeBoth said that he was going to deliver notices to three tenants who had lived in their apartments for only a year that “we are not renewing [their leases] in hopes they would naturally leave without a buyout contract.” “We appreciate your tenancy,” read one of those notices obtained by Capital & Main, “and wish you luck finding a new apartment.” But under city rent-control law, the tenants were, in fact, not required to leave. Their expiring leases would have automatically reverted to month-to-month agreements with continuing protections against evictions, city housing officials said. Sandow at the Housing Department said that the “expiration of a lease is not a legal reason to evict a tenant.” Through its attorney, K3 denied using “lease expirations as an unlawful eviction tool.” In interviews and another lawsuit filed against the company in 2024 and scheduled for trial in January, tenants also alleged that K3 employee Escobar misled them when he told them that they had to accept buyouts because their buildings would soon be demolished. The three buildings in question, two of which are in the Koreatown-East Hollywood area and one of which is in Highland Park, are still standing and occupied today. In a 2022 email to Nathan Kadisha and Qatami, K3’s director of property management, DeBoth said that “some buildings will have the narrative that we are knocking it down.” Through its attorney, K3 denied deceiving tenants about demolition as a strategy to empty buildings. Los Angeles tenant attorney Frances Campbell, who is not part of any lawsuit against K3 and who reviewed the records at Capital & Main’s request, said they would be “super strong” evidence in a civil or criminal case filed under L.A.’s Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance. Violators can be punished with steep fines and jail time. Campbell said that attempting to trick tenants into vacating their apartments, including by threatening to demolish buildings, is a tactic that comes up frequently at a legal clinic where she volunteers. “This is not the first time I’ve heard of that,” she said. “But it certainly is the first time I’ve seen a landlord put it in writing.” K3 tenant Ana Mendez said Escobar wore a light blue suit and tie when he knocked on her door in December 2022, offering her $23,000 to leave her Koreatown apartment. “He said he was from the city, and that he was offering us money to leave because they were going to demolish the building,” Mendez said in Spanish through an interpreter. Mendez turned down the money. It wasn’t enough to make her want to give up the affordable studio she shared with her children, she said, especially with the pay she earned by cleaning houses. ‘Something More Aggressive’ Castro — the former tenant from Guatemala — said that a K3 agent calling himself “Jacobo” pressed her to accept a $30,000 buyout in the fall of 2021. But Castro said she believes “Jacobo” was actually Escobar. She identified Escobar in a picture as the Jacobo she knew. Castro spoke only Spanish, but the contract Jacobo presented, she said, was written in English. Still, Castro said she turned the offer down because she could not find another affordable apartment. Her job at a pizzeria paid her in cash, so she had no pay stubs to show the next landlord. The Koreatown building where Esther Castro lived with her family. Jacobo told her the building would be demolished, too, Castro said, because it was built on an underground lake and was sinking. “If you don’t want to sign that’s fine, but we’re going to come at you with something more aggressive,” she said Jacobo told her. Soon, Jacobo and another K3 employee, who identified herself as “Johanna,” began asking about her immigration status, Castro said. “They would kind of ask in this suggesting way, like, ‘Oh, well, do you have papers?’” she said in Spanish. “‘Do you have documents?’ Castro said she grew tired of living in an empty building and of Jacobo’s relentless visits. She moved her family to Atlanta, where her money ran out within a year. “We were comfortable in Los Angeles,” Castro said, “and we arrived in Atlanta in tears.” Capital & Main

articles.title: The Political Economy of Cognitive Dissonance
articles.author: Peter Dorman
articles.content: Silkwood , a 1983 dramatization of the life of worker-activist Karen Silkwood , starring Cher, Kurt Russell and Meryl Streep, is the best and probably the only Hollywood movie about occupational safety and health. It tells the story of the transformation of Silkwood from a carefree worker in a Kerr-McGee nuclear processing plant into a soberly effective opponent of corporate malfeasance. The focus is on her, but the changing attitudes of her coworkers play an important supporting role. A wonderful detail occurs early on, when Silkwood, showing her disdain for even the minimal safety precautions in the plant, sashays up to a radiation monitor designed to flag excessive exposure and briefly flutters her hand in front of it. Later the same device will trigger intense, terrifying experiences for her. Spurred by officials of her union, the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers (OCAW), Silkwood begins to recognize that the dangers in a production system she first viewed as routine are criminally excessive. The other workers’ attitudes are mixed. Most of the workers at a union meeting with its safety experts appear to follow Silkwood’s lead, but several others, if anything, become even more accepting of the risk. OCAW wins an election to avoid decertification, but the 80–60 vote shows a substantial minority do not want to rock the boat over radiation hazards. At the beginning, worker acquiescence to risk on the job is shown to be the result of one-sided information coming from the employer in the form of bland reassurances that exposures are well below “permissible” levels. Yet when the union steps in to provide the true story, some workers, including two highlighted in the movie, refuse to believe it. They actually deny the expert evidence that their jobs may be killing them, and they take the boss’s side in the developing conflict. Anyone who has worked in struggles over unsafe working conditions will recognize this dynamic: all too often the workers most at risk resist recognizing it. They may disbelieve expert evaluation or trivialize it, or even close their eyes and ears to it altogether, rejecting the messenger rather than heeding the message. It is easy to blame them for their failure to heed and take action — easy but wrong. To understand why, we need to turn to one of the best-established concepts in psychology, cognitive dissonance. This theory, first developed in the 1950s, has many versions and extensions , but a rather general approach will be all we need. The core idea is that holding two conflicting ideas in one’s mind at the same time causes discomfort — the “dissonance” the theory is named for. This can influence behavior, although its effect will vary from one person and situation to another. Courage to Change the Things One Can A common way to avoid this dissonance is denial. This entails ignoring or disbelieving information that, if accepted, would generate mental conflict. If one is strongly committed to a particular point of view, whether political, religious or something else, it takes an effort of will to acknowledge information that contradicts it. It also shows up in the familiar reaction to disturbing news, “My child [or spouse, dog, or favored political candidate] couldn’t have done that.” There have been hundreds of studies documenting this tendency and weighing the factors that make it more or less prevalent, but little attention has been given to the one that matters most for situations like the one depicted in Silkwood : whether people believe they can act on difficult information to improve outcomes they care about. A useful way to think about the issue is to distinguish between two effects of uncomfortable information. First, it is, well, uncomfortable; one feels worse experiencing the tension it engenders in one’s mind. That’s the dissonance avoidance effect. But taking in challenging information can also help one better understand the problems one faces so to deal with them. You may not be happy to find out that your house is at greater risk of flood or fire than you thought, but armed with that knowledge you can perhaps take better precautions or explore options for moving to a safer location. You may be disturbed to find out your country is responsible for offenses against people in other parts of the world, but this can also be a basis for pooling your political influence with others who feel the same way, so together you can change these policies. The second effect, then, is the usefulness value of information: its contribution to effective action. Put this way, it becomes obvious that power, or at least the perception of it, plays a central role. Cognitive dissonance, uncomfortable as it may be, can be a step toward achieving higher goals, but only if those on the receiving end of new information and ideas feel they have the power to put them to use. To be powerless, then, is to experience the pain but not the gain, which means denial becomes a more likely response. We can see this dynamic in Silkwood. In fact, the central character’s transformation is a vivid example of the effect that growing awareness of power can create on openness to a new and uncomfortable perspective. At the beginning of the film, Karen Silkwood is portrayed as moderately knowledgeable about radiation risk, comforting an older colleague who panics after she sets off an alarm for external exposure and counseling her to get a test for internal contamination. Her approach to her own safety, however, can best be described as cavalier. But as she begins to identify more closely with her union and realizes how the hidden information she has access to can be used as leverage against the company, she takes safety much more seriously. Her sense of potential power overcomes the force of cognitive dissonance. The Cost of Denial But not so for all her coworkers. For dramatic purposes, the hostility some feel toward Silkwood is distilled down to two characters, at least one of whom is explicitly in denial over the dangers of radiation. The fear such workers express is that, by protesting, they will succeed in nothing more than getting the plant shut down, costing everyone their only hope of work in an economically depressed region of Oklahoma. From this perspective, Kerr-McGee’s workers are hostages, and if uncomfortable information about the plant is brought to light, it’s better to look the other way. In fact, that’s what happened in real life, after the events depicted in the movie: Karen Silkwood’s inside information about the cover-up of faulty fuel rod welds was revealed, and the plant was shuttered the following year. This doesn’t justify denial, of course, but it puts it in context. Economic vulnerability raises the cost of solidarity without decreasing its value, since OCAW’s efforts and that of its allies benefitted workers across the country. In a situation like this, susceptibility to denial may depend on the extent workers think in terms of “I” rather than “we.” Denial is often stark in occupational safety contexts, where the economic and health stakes for workers can be large, but it shows up in other contexts too. A strong case can be made, for instance, that it plays a role in public acquiescence to the ever-worsening climate crisis. On purely scientific grounds, 2026 should be a turning point in climate politics. Unprecedented heat waves in Europe, increasingly extreme weather in the United States and elsewhere, and a further upsurge in wildfires are making headlines, while evidence of intensified carbon cycle feedbacks is disturbing scientists . Meanwhile, a September report by the United Nations Environment Programme, Limiting Overshoot , announced that holding global warming to the Paris Agreement target of 1.5 degrees Celsius is already impossible and that we should prepare for even hotter scenarios, which we will somehow have to reverse in the coming decades. Taken together, or even separately, these should evoke an urgent activist response, but instead climate politics is moribund. Climate change is almost invisible in the US midterm elections and political battles elsewhere. Opinion polls in this country show no upsurge of alarm , as the worsening climate trails nearly all other issues as a voter concern. It would be a mistake to attribute this weird disjunction between objective danger and the lack of political response to any one factor, but cognitive dissonance is a likely contributor. There are many points of potential denial along the chain from science to politics: denial that the climate is changing at all; that its changes are due to human action (especially the burning of fossil fuels); that its effects are already harmful and are on track to become catastrophic; and that we have the tools to take action and prevent the worst. And there are also many competing economic, political and social entanglements that might make people resistant to processing the deteriorating news. One factor is worth stressing, however: the feeling of abject powerlessness . After decades of agitation and debate, the kind of climate action that might have forestalled the current crisis has remained far out of reach, leaving many with little hope that the future will be any different. If this is a common feeling, one may decide to avoid the anxiety and just skip the latest distressing news on the climate front. Facing Reality Can Fortify Mass Politics To the extent that such a dynamic is in play, we’re caught in a debilitating loop: discouragement from past political failure leads many people to pay less attention to a given problem. By paying less attention to those problems, people make continued political failure more likely. Arguably, this explains significant part of the mess we’re in. To fight discouragement, some climate activists have been making the case that, while we could be doing better politically, in economic terms things are going forward: the costs of wind and solar energy are dropping dramatically, and investment in them continues to rise. Fair enough. The intention of such sunny observations is to interrupt the denial-and-defeat loop. But it needs qualification. New green energy cuts emissions when it displaces fossil fuels, but adding capacity alone does not guarantee an overall reduction in emissions. Alas, carbon emissions have continued to rise year after year , and the infusion of wind and solar hasn’t yet bent the long-term curve of emission increase. Even worse, warming depends on cumulative emissions, so even a modest decline, much less a leveling off, won’t be enough. Annual emissions must fall and ultimately reach net zero to halt CO-driven warming. This is truly a difficult situation to find ourselves in. There are no easy answers to offer those settling into discouragement, since only a much more ambitious and resolute climate activism than we have seen has the potential to restore a sense of popular power — the conviction that we who reject the nightmare climate scenario really can force action to thwart it. Doing this will mean wedding the climate movement to a broader struggle against the suffocating power of capital, although what that entails is a story for another article. The bottom line: Power in the hands of ordinary people matters not only for what it can achieve directly but also because it encourages us to face challenges we would otherwise find it easier to ignore or deny. We are all Karen Silkwoods on the greenhouse planet we call Earth. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
