articles.title: Bombers or Solar Panels
articles.author: Paul deLespinasse
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At the very time that the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in an already gigantic military budget, the recent withdrawal of a dozen B-1 bombers from their English base suggests that a larger budget will not necessarily increase our national security. It depends on exactly what the money is spent on. The threat to the bombers in England was primarily thought to be drones launched by Iranian operatives or sympathizers. It is instructive to consider the relative costs of B-1 bombers and drones. Each B-1 bomber costs about $317,000,000—nearly one third of a billion dollars. The twelve evacuated bombers therefore were worth a total of nearly four billion dollars. As the late Senator Everett McKinley Dirksen supposedly said, “A billion here, a billion there, and pretty soon you're talking real money.” Related: Congress Should Veto-Proof Itself Military drones can cost $2,000 to perhaps $50,000, though some run much more. The Iranians have widely used Shahed-136 drones, which cost about $35,000. The disparity between the prices of B-1 bombers and the drones that threatened to destroy them in England is striking. And American forces have been using Patriot missiles (at about $4,000,000 each!) to prevent attacks by the $35,000 Iranian drones during the current war. Of course if a $4 million Patriot missile can protect a $317 million bomber or an even more expensive aircraft carrier (thirteen to fifteen billion dollars) that could make economic sense. But it would only protect the bomber or ship from one drone, and since drones are comparatively so cheap, there would probably be more than one coming in. Drone “swarms” are not to be sneered at. Buying more very expensive military equipment might therefore not be a good investment. The U.S. presently operates more than 750 military bases, like the one in England from which the B-1 bombers were withdrawn, in more than 80 foreign countries. All of these bases are vulnerable to low expense drone attacks by local people or by agents sent in from other countries. As drone technology advances, retaining this many foreign bases may need to be reconsidered. Reducing the number of these bases could save money that could be used more productively or returned to taxpayers. Our military forces clearly need to work on developing inexpensive ways to defend the remaining bases against drone attacks. We shouldn’t be using 4 million dollar missiles against cheap drones. Related: What Reading Soviet Pravda for 29 Years Taught Me About the American Press We might need to produce more drones that could be used defensively. But a better possibility might be laser weapons that could zap incoming drones for a few cents worth of electricity Under these circumstances, increasing the military budget is probably a bad idea. We need to spend defense money more wisely. Even better, we need to seek agreements with other major countries for mutual reductions in military budgets. Then we can all spend more money combating the climate disaster we are seeing all around us. A B-1 bomber, remember, costs about $317 million. Utility scale solar farms can produce electricity for about 3 to 7 cents per kilowatt-hour while reducing the need to burn coal or gas. How many solar panels could the cost of a B-1 bomber buy? You do the math.

articles.title: Language of Denial
articles.author: Norman Solomon
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Nearly two years ago, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International released in-depth reports documenting that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Months later, Israeli human rights groups did likewise. Support for Israel has declined steeply among Americans, but its defenders continue to maintain a siege of buzzwords against Palestinian rights. As historian Rashid Khalidi emphasized in his book Brokers of Deceit: How the U.S. Has Undermined Peace in the Middle East , “language matters.” Standard terms and tropes “are the essential building blocks of a lofty and solid edifice of denial of an entire narrative, of the existence of an entire people, which is basic to the affirmation of a formidable counterreality.” Prominent groups, notably the Anti-Defamation League, the American Jewish Committee, AIPAC and Christians United for Israel – along with allies in Congress, the Executive Branch and the punditocracy – rely on the same buzzwords to defame critics of Israel and deny its systematic crimes against Palestinian people. For instance: Related: Why Hollywood's Defenders of Israel Still Deny the Gaza Genocide ** “ antisemitic ” At the top in the rhetorical toolbox, a blunt instrument for smearing Israel’s critics no matter how true their accusations – and no matter the absence of evidence of bigotry against Jewish people. ** “ blood libel ” A high-dudgeon epithet for equating valid condemnations of Israel with 900-year-old antisemitic craziness. ** “ held to a higher standard ” A catchphrase to evade realities of Israel’s ongoing large-scale crimes against humanity and the fact that Israel uses enormous U.S. military aid to impose apartheid , ethnic cleansing and genocide as matters of policy. ** “ homeland for the Jewish people ” In other words: Palestinians will not replace us. Related: Why Hollywood's Defenders of Israel Still Deny the Gaza Genocide ** “ indigenous ” So, even Jewish Americans who recently moved to Israel are indigenous, unlike Palestinians whose ancestors have been living in Palestine for the last hundreds of years. ** “Jewish and democratic state ” It can’t be oxymoronic just because it’s an oxymoron. ** “ peace process ” The process of Israeli expansion that has brought war and more war, with the U.S. government functioning as “Israel’s lawyer” while arming Israel with massive quantities of weapons and continuing to make Israel (in the words of a recent Congressional Research Service report ) “the largest cumulative recipient of U.S. foreign assistance since World War II.” ** “ self-defense ” A term reserved for Israelis but certainly not Palestinians. Related: Could Ro Khanna and AOC Reshape the 2028 Democratic Primary? ** “ terrorism ” When Palestinians kill Israeli civilians but not when Israelis kill Palestinian civilians in vastly greater numbers. ** “ renounce violence ” A demand routinely made of Palestinian organizations but not of the Israeli government. ** “ Israel’s right to exist ” The standard gotcha question “Do you believe Israel has a right to exist?” can be answered with clear questions: “Do you think apartheid South Africa had a right to exist?” . . . “Do you think ethnic cleansing has a right to exist?” . . . “Do you think genocide has a right to exist?” . . . “Do you think the tens of thousands of Palestinian children killed by the Israeli military had a right to exist?”

articles.title: Hold the Line: On Nithya Raman
articles.content: This statement was approved by the Steering Committee of Reform & Revolution . The conflict between national DSA and Los Angeles DSA (DSA-LA) over the chapter’s endorsement of Nithya Raman reflects a failure of organizational unity and leadership that one resolution cannot fix. Still, we cannot fix it by never taking action. Reform & Revolution co-authored “On Nithya Raman,” the resolution brought to the DSA’s National Political Committee with comrades in Bread & Roses. This resolution affirms that DSA-LA’s endorsement was not made in compliance with R22, as the chapter never asked Raman about her support for BDS, and outlines how her record on Palestine is not in line with DSA. It asks NPC members to work with DSA-LA’s leadership on a members-only meeting by October 25th (preferably with Raman present) where she will be asked the four questions on Palestine from the national endorsement questionnaire. If the NPC then finds her to still be out of line with DSA’s anti-Zionist principles, it will vote on expelling her. Whatever the outcome, the NPC will keep assisting the chapter in supporting DSA-LA’s locally endorsed members of LA city council. The resolution documents Raman’s record in detail. In brief: She sought the endorsement of Democrats for Israel–Los Angeles in 2020, telling them she does not support BDS and believes in Israel’s right to exist, and accepted it in 2023 (DSA-LA censured her for this). In 2021 she co-authored a city resolution backing an anti-Palestinian Los Angeles Unified School District resolution, which was used to shut down a proposal by members of United Teachers Los Angeles on BDS. In 2022 she voted for Los Angeles to adopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism, which is used to attack criticisms of Zionism and Israel. She publicly rejected national DSA’s public statement after October 7th, 2023. In addition, this year on October 7th, she posted a statement condemning the attacks with no mention of the genocide in Gaza. This year in September, when asked at a Jewish Federation forum on where she differs from DSA on BDS, she said it was not part of her platform and that she has “been vocal about places where I’ve disagreed with the DSA on a range of issues.” These are Zionist positions, and they are what R22 was written to address. Not only is Raman in technical violation of R22, she is actively opposed to DSA’s positions and goals. Agreement with BDS does not even fully encompass DSA’s own positions on this matter; that Raman cannot publicly support BDS beyond not supporting prosecution for it goes below even our most basic expectations of any candidate. This resolution deliberately keeps to R22 and Palestine. This is her most specific violation, and the one for which DSA has a clear convention mandate. However, Raman’s endorsement is opportunistic for many reasons beyond her positions on Palestine. The question underlying the national debate around Nithya Raman is not solely about whether national DSA must discipline Raman and DSA-LA due to a convention resolution (though that is, of course, part of it). The important question is does Raman represent DSA and our democratic socialist politics . Even if we understand that DSA may endorse candidates that do not fully represent our positions to grow the workers’ movement, Raman’s shortcomings are more likely to disorient people outside of DSA about the character and positions we hold – and harm our ability to be credible partners in the movement against Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people. Raman is not a socialist, and from an objective standpoint she has always had a tenuous relationship with DSA-LA at best. She does not publicly call herself a socialist or advocate for socialism. Apart from DSA-LA’s endorsement, neither socialism nor DSA appear in her campaign’s material. In fact, when the chapter endorsed her, she welcomed DSA-LA as “joining our broad coalition of Angelenos,” and when asked directly whether she is a capitalist on CNN, responded with only: “We are in a capitalist system. It’s a city government.” At least outside of LA, this largely flew under the radar of top concerns when her office was smaller. Now she is making national headlines. We need to consider and be very clear about what it would mean for her independent “progressive” message to be the leading voice of DSA, especially in California and particularly as we approach the terrain of the 2027-2028 presidential election cycle. A candidate this far out of line with our program (by her own admission) carrying DSA-LA’s full-throated endorsement would be alarming even if the red lines of R22 had never been adopted . In response to these concerns, comrades in DSA may argue that other candidates endorsed by their chapters may also be out of line with our program or not publicly message as socialists. We acknowledge this – but this isn’t an answer to the problem in front of us. That there are issues with candidates representing DSA does not in any way mean that we can simply ignore a candidate of Raman’s notoriety and egregious opposition to our political program and goals. Still, we should build an organization whose candidates represent us properly, not just those who have a large enough platform or are in dramatic opposition. In order to do this, the NPC must take the plunge and provide the leadership needed to cohere our national project, not to ignore the most obvious and public violators because of the precedent that might be set by acting. Despite Raman’s violations of our policies being clear, nothing in the decision of how to proceed is obvious, especially if we wish to center not only what is best for DSA, but what is best for the socialist movement as a whole. The difficult situation we are in is the result of indecisive leadership and the broader underdevelopment of DSA as a party. Enforcing R22 here is necessary from a moral and political standpoint: there is a genocide being perpetrated in Palestine, and we do not want people supporting the state responsible for it to be representing our organization. But enforcement is also purely punitive. This conversation, by definition, is only happening because an endorsement has already been made – one almost entirely unaccountable to the rest of the organization. By the time a chapter has endorsed a candidate with a record of Zionist positions and we need to invoke R22, we have already lost some trust from our allies in the Palestinian liberation movement and we have to contend with reversing a vote by a chapter’s membership. The strength of political red lines is not in our ability to enforce them, but in our ability to cohere around them to have a strong, inspiring, and unified message to working people. This not only grows our ability to publicly advocate our political positions with consistency, but also can itself be inspiring to the millions of working people entering political struggle and consciousness. Coherence around our principles is not won by simply utilizing red lines as a hammer. For instance, Zohran Mamdani’s success in campaigning as an anti-Zionist did not come from a red line being enforced on NYC-DSA. It came from a chapter that was able to politically, organizationally, and structurally unite behind his campaign in the face of reactionary forces attempting to discredit him for his views on Palestine and his alignment with DSA. To build that political and organizational capacity, we must prioritize cadre development, candidates and campaigns accountable to DSA (not just the whims of a candidate), independent electoral and organizing infrastructure separate from the Democratic Party, and nationally centralized and democratically decided endorsement standards. Bodies like the NPC and the National Electoral Committee must be able to integrate chapters into our broader national political apparatus. The development of our electoral apparatus will not happen all at once. Inevitably, chapters who are beginning their electoral work or who have generally had lax endorsement standards will exist. We can differentiate between imperfect DSA cadre candidates (candidates who view DSA as their primary constituency and want to represent our politics, but who may struggle with doing so properly) and candidates who view DSA as simply a part of their progressive coalition and do not meaningfully intend to represent us. That first group may fail to become “great” DSA electeds, but at least part of the blame will be ours. How could we expect them to succeed without a coherent political leadership and campaigning mass party to support them? The latter should be avoided, and assisting chapters in developing the ability and political will to avoid the short-term benefits of these endorsements is incumbent on the national organization as much as it is on the members across the country. Towards this, an important material step will be the ongoing establishment of Federal Socialists In Office structures. More than being just for accountability, however, an FSIO committee must be designed to integrate our electoral projects into DSA’s national campaigns and movements, especially as they relate to our relationship to unions and organized labor. We need to develop the structures that allow electeds to support each other, for the NPC and national committees to support electeds, and for rank-and-file DSA members to have a democratic voice in our electoral project at a national scale . In that sense, our work going forward needs to be oriented less towards reactively bringing candidates in line and more towards proactively uniting DSA behind a national, democratically-directed electoral strategy. Candidates and endorsed campaigns, though an important part of that strategy, should not be individually so important that any critique of those candidates or campaigns feels like it may potentially destabilize and collapse DSA’s project as a whole. In order to actually turn DSA into a mass party of the working class with this level of unity around our political goals and campaigns, we need to acknowledge that these deficiencies are not just the result of organizational underdevelopment. US politics heavily centers the desires and programs of individual candidates, and most organizations give political endorsements liberally on vague political alignment. Naturally, those new to the socialist movement may wonder why we need to hold firm on this or that red line or standard when faced with the excitement of a campaign, with the membership growth driven by them, and with the prospect of defeating this or that terrible politician. Even if comrades agree theoretically or morally with red lines or other standards, they will not immediately see the positive reasons for having a strictly defined political program uniting campaigns unless we can demonstrate the power that a unified and credible message gives us. Without this, as we’ve seen throughout Biden’s term in office, the temptation of effecting short-term change and being a part of the “governing coalition” will lead to our inability to fight for a working class platform in a way that excites our own members and those entering political consciousness. If we wish not to squander our 2025 and 2026 growth, we must seriously contend with what it takes to actually build – not just wish for – the lasting institutions and structures that would allow us to flex our collective power in the long, permanent term. Members are invested in DSA as a big socialist tent. We can only build party-like accountability structures under this big tent by bringing it together proactively , before we encounter difficult situations like this one . Opportunistic pressure is often agnostic to professed political positions, and it can only be combated through actual mass work and party-building. Therefore, R22 may be the necessary thing to invoke now, at this stage, but it is difficult to say that this situation is not of our own making in key respects. R22 mandates that members who consistently and publicly oppose BDS and the Palestinian cause are subject to expulsion by a two-thirds vote of the NPC, regardless of their endorsement status. In practice, that only really matters for members endorsed for or elected to office, and R22’s red lines have always been understood as red lines for candidates. The NPC already sent a letter to DSA-LA asking about the political positions of Raman and concerns they have about her endorsement. In response, DSA-LA sent a letter that argues that Raman, despite previous violation of our standards, is in line with R22. The claims are dubious at best. Frankly, the actual political positions Raman publicly holds have not changed, and the arguments DSA-LA’s leadership make do not actually address the clear-cut violations of R22, though they point out some less bad positions she now has, such as being opposed to prosecuting BDS. Nithya Raman is still obviously not in alignment with the positions mandated by our National Convention, the highest decision-making body of our organization, and is subject to discipline under that mandate. We are not “excited” in any capacity to be forced to potentially expel a member of DSA, especially when there was an opportunity to come together under our program and fight for socialist politics in a city as large as Los Angeles. Beyond that, we do not believe that it is proper to immediately begin with expulsion for someone who does not align with a policy – even one as important as R22. That is why the NPC proposal we support does not immediately expel Raman. It starts with a conversation among DSA-LA’s members, and it gives Raman a fair chance to either argue that she is in agreement with our positions on Palestine, or to come into alignment with our politics. What would it take to come into alignment with DSA and rectify these concerns? In such a conversation, it should be noted that part of the issue came from DSA-LA’s own failure to adequately prepare Raman on our policies. R22 does not just require candidates to not say they are Zionists. It requires that they be asked about BDS and Palestinian liberation during the endorsement process , and expects them to positively promote anti-Zionist positions when asked. Regarding the claims by DSA-LA on Raman’s current positions on BDS: she may be willing to not actively attack BDS or our positions, but she is not willing to positively advocate for them either. Because of her previous positions and associations with Zionist organizations, a public, positive declaration of a change in position, of support for the BDS movement and for Palestinian liberation, is needed in order to assuage rightful concerns . A declaration of support for BDS made only in internal DSA spaces will not resolve the core issue. Our position as a caucus is that we are in favor of enforcing red lines after an exhaustive process has been attempted in good faith. This resolution continues and officially defines that process. Any situation that requires the NPC to enforce standards on chapters will necessarily put the national organization against a chapter’s majority. In this case, the national organization is not just the elected leadership, but the highest decision-making body of DSA: its National Convention, with representatives from every chapter in the country. In order to effectively enforce the standards that we have collectively set as an organization, and after exhausting attempts to work with the comrades in a given chapter in good faith and genuine dialogue, national must be able to contradict and even overturn the errant decisions of a chapter majority. Some may worry about a split, but we believe this misses an obvious fact: if an ideological split has already happened, and a chapter is using the name of DSA in a way that contradicts our democratically adopted program, it is better to rebuke them than to let them operate independently, hoping to avoid a split that has already happened. We doubt that most DSA-LA members who voted to endorse Raman are Zionists. Ideally, we would like to help them (and any other chapters in a similar predicament) in whatever ways are necessary to build their chapter as an important arm of a national party. Part of that involves thinking about how to best push for and promote our program in their local context and political terrain while maintaining political and organizational independence from forces who do not support it. Chapters such as Portland, for instance, have experimented with endorsement tiers. In regards to the potential of an AOC run for President, we have proposed an independent endorsement campaign, with our own canvasses, data-collection, literature, scripts, and so on – this could be another way to handle the contradictions of exciting and important but external electoral campaigns that are attracting the attention of the working class. Both are ways that non-DSA or non-socialist candidates can be supported for the aspects of their campaigns that connect to and energize the working class while still maintaining our program, mandate, and principles. None of this can be fixed by one resolution. The debacle around Nithya Raman is in part caused by the broader crisis of organization in the working class. While difficult, many of these issues are necessary and normal to confront in the historical development of a working class movement. However, the “left” NPC majority (ourselves included) has so far failed to deliver the decisive Marxist leadership necessary to navigate this complicated situation, both out of caution and disorientation. In an ideologically diverse and de facto federal organization like DSA, the prospect of taking the unprecedented step to discipline a candidate that has been endorsed by the majority of one of our largest chapters is daunting. There are real costs to this course of action, even if we believe it is necessary and for the long-term health of our movement. But hesitation has costs too, and caution is not neutral. Trotsky described the task of revolutionaries as overcoming “the contradiction between the maturity of the objective revolutionary conditions and the immaturity of the proletariat and its vanguard.” The Raman endorsement is a zoom-in on that contradiction: conditions now exist for DSA to contest mayoral elections in the largest cities in the country, but our organization is not yet mature enough to ensure that those candidates, or campaigns, are our own. Closing that gap will take more than a Marxist majority on the NPC. It will take thousands of Marxists engaged in mass work, united in one democratic party of the working class. Getting there will inevitably involve learning from many mistakes. It is up to Marxist leadership to guide the “party” through those mistakes with stern patience, and that includes making hard decisions before they are made for us. That is why we co-authored this resolution, and why we will keep fighting for a DSA that will make the next one unnecessary.

articles.title: Chattel Slavery vs. Wage Labor: Who Is Really Free?
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 1860, nearly four million Black people were enslaved in the United States. Their labor produced enormous wealth, but they had virtually no control over what they made or who benefited from it. They planted and harvested cotton, cultivated tobacco and sugar, built homes, maintained households, and practiced skilled trades. Today, American workers produce goods and services on a scale unimaginable in 1860. Yet millions struggle to afford housing, healthcare, education, childcare, food, and retirement. The question connecting these eras is not whether the systems are the same. They are profoundly different. It is this: Who controls the wealth people create, and who is really free? Two Systems, Different Forms of Power Under chattel slavery, people were legally treated as property. They could be bought, sold, separated from their families, and subjected to violence. They could not freely leave or negotiate the terms of their labor. Wage workers, by contrast, are legally free. In theory, they can change employers, negotiate pay, organize unions, own property, and exercise political rights. Those freedoms matter. But legal freedom does not guarantee economic independence. People with little access to land, capital, or other sources of income generally have to sell their labor to survive. When necessities depend on a paycheck, refusing unfavorable work can be difficult. Critics have called this condition wage slavery . The phrase should not erase the violence and total denial of personhood at the heart of chattel slavery. It points instead to a question about economic power: How much control can people exercise over their lives when they depend on owners and employers for access to work and income? The 1860 Debate—and the Civil War By 1860, slavery and wage labor were expanding in different parts of the country. Southern enslavers defended an economy built on forced Black labor. In the North, factories, railroads, commercial agriculture, and wage employment were growing. The fight to expand slavery—and the political power of enslavers—helped drive the nation toward civil war. The conflict was not a balanced contest between two equivalent labor systems; slavery was central to secession and the war that followed. www.nps.gov Still, people at the time debated the insecurity of wage labor. Proslavery writer George Fitzhugh argued that Northern employers treated workers more cruelly than enslavers treated people they held in bondage. He claimed enslavers had a paternalistic duty to provide for them, while employers could dismiss workers when they were no longer profitable. Fitzhugh was not calling for workers’ liberation. He used the risks of wage dependence to defend human bondage, while ignoring slavery’s violence, family separation, sexual exploitation, and denial of personhood. His argument nevertheless shows that the unequal power between employers and workers was already a subject of public debate. Abraham Lincoln imagined a different possibility. In an 1859 address, he described wage work as a stage from which a person might earn, save, acquire tools or land, and eventually work independently. His vision assumed workers could move beyond dependence on wages. abrahamlincolnonline.org That path was never open to everyone, and it became harder to follow as industrial capitalism grew. But the shift toward wage dependence was not simply inevitable. Worker-owned cooperatives and other forms of shared ownership could have let people produce at scale while retaining collective control over their lives, their work and its rewards. Political choices could have supported those alternatives. Emancipation Without Resources The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, except as punishment for a crime following conviction. But legal freedom did not return to formerly enslaved people the land, wealth, or authority they had been denied. In Life and Times of Frederick Douglass , Douglass describes formerly enslaved people being turned out of their quarters and left to find food and shelter. He writes that they were “without food, without shelter, without land, without money, and without friends,” and describes them as “naked to the open sky.” en.wikisource.org The episode makes the former enslavers’ sense of ownership starkly visible. Even after emancipation, some acted as though the land and shelter where people had lived—and the resources needed to survive—still belonged to them. Douglass’s account shows how little emancipation alone changed the material power of those who had controlled people’s labor and lives. That history matters to this article because freedom is not only a legal status. It also depends on whether people have the resources and power to make meaningful choices. Wage Labor Won—but It Wasn’t the Only Option Today, paid employment is the predominant way people earn a living. For much of American history, however, people worked on farms, in family enterprises, or in independent trades. As wage employment expanded, more people rented their time and labor to employers, surrendering some control over how their lives and work was organized and who received its proceeds. That transition helped build extraordinary productive capacity in the United States. It also concentrated decision-making into the hands of the elite. In many workplaces, owners and executives determine what gets made, how work is organized, and whether workers keep their jobs. The wealth that is extracted by those businesses is generated by labor. It is a collective effort, but authority over that wealth is often concentrated in relatively few hands. The Collective Makes the Fortune We are often told that hard work guarantees success: work hard, make the right choices, and you will get ahead. But effort alone does not determine who becomes wealthy. Ownership does. Workers make goods and provide services. Consumers create markets by buying them. Families provide care that sustains workers and raises the next generation. Taxpayers support infrastructure, education, research, and public institutions businesses rely on. Great fortunes depend on this broad, collective contribution, even when the returns flow disproportionately to owners and investors. By fall 2026, public estimates had placed Elon Musk’s net worth above $1 trillion, largely reflecting the value of his ownership stakes. Such estimates can change with markets, but the scale points to a larger concern: concentrated wealth can bring concentrated power. businessinsider.com Billionaires—and a person valued at over a trillion dollars—can make decisions that reshape workplaces and livelihoods, including firing large numbers of workers. The criticism is not that owners have no role in building companies. It is that legal ownership can give a few people sweeping authority over enterprises whose success depends on the work of many. Workers can be treated as disposable while the people who control the assets act as though the wealth belongs to them alone. Ordinary people are not to blame for participating. People work, shop, and pay bills within a system where opting out can mean losing access to necessities. The danger is that our essential participation helps build private power over which we have little say—and that power can then shape the conditions under which we live and work. Who Is Really Free? Under chattel slavery, the law assigned control of labor and its proceeds to enslavers. Under contemporary capitalism, much of the power to direct production rests with owners, investors, and executives. Workers can organize; government can regulate and redistribute; cooperatives and public institutions can provide alternatives. Those possibilities depend on political choices. The United States abolished the legal ownership of human beings without ending the concentration of economic power. It developed extraordinary productive capacity without ensuring that everyone shares in its benefits. America can produce enormous wealth. The question is whether the people who produce it will gain enough power to decide what it is for—and who benefits. Emancipation ended the legal ownership of human beings. The struggle for economic democracy asks what freedom requires beyond that.

articles.title: Car Accident Claims
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California’s comparative fault rules allow people injured in car accidents to seek compensation even when they share some responsibility for the crash, although their compensation may be reduced by their percentage of fault. Ventura, California, is a coastal city where drivers travel along busy roads, local streets, and major routes such as Highway 101. Traffic congestion, changing road conditions, and driver mistakes can contribute to collisions throughout the area. After a crash, consulting a Ventura, CA, car accident lawyer can help an injured person understand how fault may affect an insurance claim or personal injury lawsuit. California follows a pure comparative negligence system. Under this rule, an injured person can recover damages even if they are found to be mostly responsible for an accident. However, the amount awarded is reduced according to their share of fault. Understanding California’s Comparative Fault Rule Comparative fault is used when more than one person may have contributed to an accident. For example, one driver might have been speeding while another made an unsafe turn. Investigators, insurance companies, or a court may consider the actions of both drivers when determining responsibility. California’s system differs from rules in states that prevent people from recovering damages if their share of fault reaches a particular threshold. In California, a person may still recover compensation even if they are found 90% responsible, although the recovery would be reduced substantially. The legal foundation for this principle includes the California Supreme Court’s decision in Li v. Yellow Cab Co. (1975), which adopted comparative negligence in California. How Shared Fault Can Reduce Compensation The percentage of fault assigned to an injured person directly affects the damages they may recover. Consider a situation in which a driver suffers $100,000 in total damages but is found 20% responsible for the accident. If the remaining 80% of responsibility belongs to another party, the injured driver’s recoverable damages would generally be reduced to $80,000. The calculation is straightforward, but determining the correct percentage of fault can be more complicated. Each party may present different accounts of the collision, and the available evidence may support more than one interpretation. Insurance companies may argue that an injured driver was speeding, distracted, or failed to take reasonable steps to avoid a crash. The injured person may dispute that assessment based on witness accounts, photographs, vehicle damage, or other evidence . Evidence Can Help Establish Responsibility Evidence plays an important role in determining how an accident happened. Useful records may include: Police or collision reports. Photographs and videos of the scene and vehicle damage. Statements from eyewitnesses . Traffic camera or dashcam footage. Medical records documenting accident-related injuries. Expert analysis when the circumstances require it. Drivers should preserve relevant evidence and provide accurate information when reporting an accident. They should avoid guessing about details they cannot remember or making assumptions about fault before the facts are clear. How Insurance Companies Evaluate Fault Insurance adjusters review available information to assess liability and the value of a claim. They may consider traffic laws, driver statements, damage patterns, medical documentation, and other relevant records. An adjuster’s initial assessment is not necessarily the final determination of fault. If the parties disagree, additional evidence or legal proceedings may be needed to resolve the dispute. Before accepting a settlement, an injured person should understand what expenses and losses it covers. A settlement agreement may also limit the ability to seek additional compensation for the same accident later. Why Legal Guidance May Help Car accident claims can involve disputed facts, medical expenses, lost income, and disagreements about future losses. Legal guidance can help an injured person understand California’s comparative fault system, organize supporting evidence, and evaluate a settlement offer. A lawyer can also explain the possible effect of shared responsibility on a claim and identify deadlines that may apply. Under California Code of Civil Procedure Section 335.1, the general deadline for filing many personal injury lawsuits is two years from the date of injury, although exceptions may apply. Claims involving government entities can have much shorter deadlines. Key Takeaways California follows a pure comparative negligence system. An injured person can generally seek damages even if they share responsibility for a collision. Compensation is reduced according to the injured person’s percentage of fault. Police reports, photographs, witness statements, and medical records may help establish what happened. Legal deadlines and settlement terms should be reviewed carefully.

articles.title: Titanium Over Traditional Option
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Men approach jewellery with great consideration of compatibility with what they always do. That’s the short answer to the curiosity behind the preference for titanium rings. Those who always get dirt on their hands or have to work with harsh machinery know that their job can easily destroy an expensive soft gold band within weeks. But if that isn’t enough reason to convince, here’s a list of more rationale behind the shift to this particular metal. Scratch and Dent Resistance As we pointed out, gold is soft. It’s one of the reasons why they work well in fine jewellery. However, it’s also the reason why they easily pick up dents and scratches from daily manual work. Just seeing it withstand the test of time doesn’t mean it’s durable in any practical sense. You buy them with hopes they’d stay pristine. By choosing mens titanium rings , wearers don’t have to worry about visible damage. They hold their finish under conditions that would visibly damage gold and other traditional metals. The sturdiness of titanium jewellery resists small impacts or scratches when working with rough materials. Give it a year and the titanium piece stays close to how it looked on day one. This is something you cannot say about gold or silver bands. Weight That Doesn’t Interfere With Grip or Dexterity A heavy ring becomes a genuine hindrance for anyone whose hands need to move precisely and repeatedly through a working day. Let’s say platinum, in particular. This material is dense enough to make it heavier to the finger. Men who use a lot of their hands for work would find it very distracting. Titanium is lighter than platinum and other traditional jewellery materials. A ring made out of it can be worn with a solid, substantial profile without adding the weight that a similarly sized ring in a traditional metal would carry. So if you plan to work without having a repeated look at your ring finger, titanium should be your choice of metal for a wedding band. Corrosion Resistance Against Oil, Sweat, and Chemical Exposure Cleaning chemicals and engine oil, even fluid as simple as sweat, can cause tarnishing on jewellery. Silver is vulnerable under this kind of exposure, and some gold alloys can react with some chemicals that cause them to lose their finish over time. Meanwhile, titanium resists corrosion from most chemicals that you can see in workplaces and households. It doesn’t react with sweat and most industrial chemicals either. If you worry too much about discolouration due to exposure to chemicals and your own sweat, titanium shields itself from that kind of chemical degradation. A Safety Profile Better Than Traditional Metals This is the reason that carries the most weight for men working around machinery. A ring caught on rotating equipment or heavy tools can cause serious injury. Sometimes, the wearer is at the mercy of the way a metal responds to a catastrophic force. Standard titanium rings are engineered to bend or break under extreme force. This is a good safety consideration for men working around power tools and heavy machinery. If needed, they can be torn away from the wearer's body by professionals and emergency respondents using the right tools. Meanwhile, gold or platinum bands are more malleable. They will deform and constrict on the wearer at times when you don’t need them to. Durability That Justifies the Cost Over a Working Lifetime A gold band that gets scratched, dented, and eventually needs resizing or repolishing carries an ongoing cost most buyers don’t factor in at the point of purchase. Titanium’s resistance to scratching and denting means a well-made titanium ring can be worn daily for decades without needing the kind of maintenance that softer metals require. For a man who’s going to wear the same ring through years of manual work, the upfront cost comparison against gold or platinum misses the point. The relevant comparison is what the ring looks like, and costs to maintain, five or ten years into daily wear. On that measure, titanium consistently comes out ahead for anyone whose hands don’t get an easy day at the office.

articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Memory loss changes how a person moves through the day, manages medication, and responds to unfamiliar situations. Specialized memory care combines supervision with familiar routines, calm spaces, and support matched to cognitive needs. Staff monitor health, guide personal care, and respond quickly when confusion or distress appears. These practices protect safety while preserving dignity, choice, and comfort. Daily details show why the right setting matters for families and residents alike. Why Specialized Memory Care Matters Memory care begins with a setting arranged around predictable needs. Clear paths, visible common areas, and consistent staff routines reduce hazards when a resident forgets directions or misjudges a situation. Families researching memory care in Meridian, ID , should ask how each residence handles supervision, personal care, medication reminders, meals, and nighttime concerns. Those answers show whether daily support is practical, respectful, and consistent. General senior living communities support people with varying levels of independence, while memory care addresses cognitive changes directly. Staff learn each resident’s habits, communication style, and signs of distress. That knowledge helps them respond before confusion becomes a safety concern. Safety Built Into Daily Routines A steady daily schedule helps residents recognize what comes next. Regular times for waking, meals, activities, personal care, and rest reduce unnecessary decisions and limit confusion. When routines stay consistent, staff also notice changes in appetite, mood, sleep, balance, or behavior. Familiar Structure Reduces Confusion Visual cues help residents who struggle with memory or verbal instructions. Large signs, recognizable room features, and uncluttered walkways help residents find essential areas with less frustration. Staff use short explanations and calm reminders instead of rushing through tasks. A familiar activity schedule gives the day a clear rhythm. Simple choices, such as selecting a sweater or joining a music session, preserve personal control without creating excessive demands. Support With Movement and Health Falls often follow changes in balance, vision, strength, or judgment. Memory care staff watch how residents move between rooms, rise from chairs, and use mobility aids. They report changes to family members and healthcare providers, so care plans remain current. Medication support adds another layer of protection. Staff follow prescribed schedules, document administration when required, and watch for changes that need medical attention. Ask how a residence coordinates medication management , appointments, and urgent health concerns. Comfort Through Person-Centered Care Safety works best when residents feel known and respected. Staff who recognize personal preferences can approach bathing, dressing, meals, and bedtime with less resistance. Familiar music, photographs, foods, and conversation topics also support emotional comfort. Personal care should protect privacy and dignity. Staff can explain each step, allow extra time, and adjust communication when a resident feels anxious. A calm approach reduces pressure and gives the resident room to participate. Meaningful activities support comfort throughout the day. Walking, folding laundry, gardening, crafts, or listening to music can connect with earlier interests. Activities should match ability and attention span, with staff ready to simplify or change the task. A Safer Setting for Families Family members need clear information about daily care, especially when a resident cannot describe every experience. Regular updates can cover meals, sleep, participation, mood, mobility, and health changes. Direct communication helps families recognize patterns and make informed care decisions. Visits work better when staff shares useful context. A family member might learn that a resident responds well to a familiar song or prefers quieter mornings. Staff can use that information during daily interactions, creating consistency between family visits and regular care. Families should tour a residence during an ordinary activity period instead of relying on a polished presentation. They can observe whether staff speak respectfully, residents receive prompt help, and common spaces remain calm. Questions about staffing, emergency procedures, care assessments, and family communication deserve direct answers. Conclusion Specialized memory care supports safety through predictable routines, attentive supervision, medication coordination, and surroundings that reduce confusion. It supports comfort through familiar activities, respectful personal care, and communication shaped around each resident. Families can begin their search by touring residences, asking how staff respond to changing needs, and reviewing the daily care process in detail. Those steps help identify a setting that protects health while preserving independence, dignity, and connection.
